Il ordonne au Prophète ﷺ de L'adorer et de placer en Lui sa confiance, et assure que son Seigneur n'est pas inattentif à ce que font les hommes. Les commentateurs le considèrent comme la conclusion de la sourate Hud, après les récits des prophètes et les menaces adressées aux incrédules.

Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et Ibn al-Jawzi expliquent que le « ghayb » désigne ce qui est caché aux créatures, et que Dieu rétribue l'homme de bien comme le malfaiteur. Ibn 'Abbas et al-Dahhak y voient les trésors des cieux et de la terre ou tout ce qui échappe aux serviteurs, tandis que d'autres comprennent la descente du châtiment depuis le ciel et son surgissement de la terre ; Abu 'Ali al-Farisi retient ce dernier sens en considérant la construction comme une extension de langage.

Les exégètes s'accordent à dire que la mention de l'adoration avant la confiance indique que celle-ci n'est utile qu'accompagnée de celle-là. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi et al-Baydawi notent que le « fa » exprime la conséquence de l'affirmation que tout retourne à Dieu. Sur le plan des lectures, Nafi' et Hafs lisent « yurja'u » à la voix passive, tandis que les autres lisent « yarji'u » ; et plusieurs lisent « ta'malun » à la deuxième personne, les autres « ya'malun ».

Ka'b al-Ahbar rapporte que la fin de la Torah correspond à la fin de Hud, et certains hadiths cités sur les mérites de la sourate ne font pas l'unanimité. Al-Tabari et al-Baghawi rappellent que la verse console le Prophète et menace les mécréants, tandis qu'Ibn 'Ashur la juge comme un épilogue qui résume la sourate.
en: The commentators explain that this verse describes the Qur'an as a book whose verses are firmly composed, free of flaw or contradiction, then clearly detailed, all coming from the All-Wise, All-Aware Lord. There is broad agreement that ihkam means perfection of composition and freedom from defect, and that tafsil means clear explanation. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that the verses are perfect both in wording and meaning. The disagreement concerns how these two terms are understood. Al-Hasan al-Basri takes ihkam as the command and prohibition and tafsil as promise and warning, while Qatada sees ihkam as protection from falsehood followed by the clarification of the lawful and the unlawful. Mujahid takes tafsil simply as explanation. Al-Tabari adopts a view that joins freedom from defect and falsehood with the distinction between commands and prohibitions. Al-Mawardi lists five possible readings, one of which extends ihkam to the whole text. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari mention the coherence of the text, the absence of abrogation, the division into surahs and verses, or the gradual revelation. Ibn Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari hold that the particle thumma marks a progression in rank rather than in time. As for min ladun hakim khabir, some read it as meaning from the presence of, and others attach it to both verbs. The disjointed letters at the start are understood in various ways: some leave their meaning to God, others see names of surahs or a sign of the Qur'an's inimitability.

This verse states that the Book, whose verses are firmly established and clearly explained, came from the All-Wise, All-Aware for one purpose: that none be worshipped but God alone. The Prophet ﷺ is described as a warner of God's punishment to those who disobey and a bearer of good news of His reward to those who obey. The commentators differ on the grammar of the particle 'an'. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan take it as explanatory, meaning 'namely', while al-Farra, al-Zajjaj, al-Nasafi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Alusi take it as a purposive or verbal conjunction, with an implied preposition, or as a separate sentence in which the Prophet addresses people with a command to affirm the oneness of God. On the meaning of 'ihkam' (firm establishment), Ibn Abbas understood it as not being abrogated by another book, Qatada as being free of falsehood, and al-Hasan and Abu al-'Aliya as command and prohibition. Mujahid held that the verses were first perfected as a whole and then explained one by one. Most exegetes, including Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, understand worship of God as affirming His oneness and rejecting association. Al-Sha'rawi notes that the negation followed by affirmation first rejects falsehood and then establishes truth, while Ibn 'Ashur sees the warning as answering the prohibition and the good news as answering the command. Commentators also debate whether the pronoun 'minhu' refers to God or to the Book. The verse thus joins the restriction to monotheism with the affirmation of the prophetic mission in the form of warning and good news.

This verse calls people to ask their Lord for forgiveness for their past sins and polytheism, and then to turn back to Him in obedience. In return, it promises that they will be given a good provision of life until a set term, and that every person of merit will receive the reward of his merit. Those who turn away are warned of the punishment of a great day. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that the istighfar here primarily concerns shirk, then other sins, and that repentance means returning to obedience and resolving not to fall back into sin. Ibn Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari note that the word "thumma" marks a ranking, since giving up idolatry takes precedence over seeking forgiveness. Most commentators take the set term to be death, while Sa'id ibn Jubayr takes it to be the Day of Resurrection. On the good provision, some describe it as contentment with what is easy and patience with what is decreed, others as ease of living and good health, and Ibn Atiyya as the believer's joy in hoping in God. On the reward of merit, Ibn Abbas and Mujahid take it as the reward for good deeds, Qatada as the recompense in the Hereafter, and Ibn Mas'ud points out that one good deed is worth ten. The great day is, for most, the Day of Resurrection, though some think of the Battle of Badr or the hardships of this world.

The commentators explain that this part of the verse states that the final return of all people is to Allah alone, who will call them to account and repay them, and that He is able to do all things, including raising them after death and punishing them for their association with others. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and al-Sa'di agree that the passage warns the polytheists who are being called to the oneness of God and to repentance, that the notion of return refers to death followed by resurrection for judgment, and that the verse is both a threat and a justification for fearing the great day.

Ibn 'Ashur sees the sentence as the reason for the fear expressed earlier: those addressed are heading toward God's power and cannot escape it. He notes that the word return can cover the return after death, even though the polytheists do not accept it. Al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan specify that this refers to the return on that day. Al-Razi observes that the phrase 'to Allah is your return' implies exclusivity, since no one else governs or disposes in the hereafter. He considers that mentioning the return together with absolute power is at once a fearsome threat and a good tiding, because the One who is all-powerful can rescue the weak person on the brink of ruin.

Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Jaza'iri and al-Qasimi connect the verse to the context that follows, which describes those who bent their chests and covered themselves with their garments, thinking they were hiding from God, a behaviour they judge to be ignorance since God knows what they conceal and what they reveal. The commentators agree that the meaning of the verse is clear and that it raises no particular legal points. Al-Sa'di stresses that God's power over all things includes the resurrection of the dead, while al-Alusi presents the verse as a reinforcement of the mention of the great day.

This verse describes people who fold their chests and wrap their heads in their garments, thinking they can hide from God or from the Prophet ﷺ; God answers that He knows what they conceal and what they reveal, for He knows fully what the breasts contain. Al-Tabari understands the folding of the chest as turning away from truth, doubt, or concealed hostility, and stresses that these people imagined God would not know their hidden intentions; al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi read it as a picture of swerving away from the truth, while Mujahid speaks of doubt and suspicion regarding the truth and al-Hasan of the disbelief their hearts conceal. As for the occasion of revelation, al-Mawardi and al-Wahidi link it to al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, a man of sweet speech who hid his enmity, following Ibn Abbas, whereas Abd Allah ibn Shaddad ascribes it to hypocrites who turned away whenever they passed the Prophet. On the meaning of covering oneself with garments, opinions differ: most take it as wrapping the head, others as the night or as hiding a concern within, and al-Tabari adds reluctance to hear God's word. The commentators agree on the central point: God's knowledge encompasses both the secret and the open, so concealment cannot escape Him.

This verse states that God provides for every creature that moves on the earth, whether human or animal, and that He knows where each one settles and where it is entrusted. The commentators agree that the word dabba refers to any creature that crawls or walks on the ground, and that rizq means whatever sustains life and food. The phrase 'upon God' is understood by most as a grace rather than a strict obligation, though the wording is used to confirm that the promise will certainly be kept. Mujahid adds that what reaches a creature comes from God, and that some animals may die of hunger if no provision reaches them. All agree that everything is written in the Preserved Tablet, though some take the Clear Book to mean God's knowledge itself.

Opinions differ on the meaning of 'mustaqarr' and 'mustawda''. Ibn 'Abbas, as transmitted by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, takes it as the place where the creature rests and the place where it dies or is buried. Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Mas'ud link these terms to the womb and the loins, or to the moment of death. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas understands them as the days of life and the place of death and resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi prefer the dwelling place on earth and the place where the creature existed before settling. Others take the resting place to be paradise or hell and the deposit to be the grave.

Al-Tabari explains his preference by the verse's focus on sustenance, and he argues that the knowledge of where creatures are provided for follows naturally from this. Ibn Kathir, citing al-Tabari, notes the same reasoning.

This verse states that God created the heavens and the earth in six days, and that His Throne was upon the water before that, and that creation serves to test people to see who acts best. The commentators agree that the Throne and the water existed before the heavens and earth. Most take the days as days of this world, while Ka'b al-Ahbar holds them to be days of the Hereafter, each a thousand years. On the meaning of the Throne being upon the water, Mujahid and Qatada say it was so before anything else was created, and Ibn 'Abbas says the water rested on the back of the wind. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud read it as meaning only that nothing stood between them, and al-Alusi discusses this view at length. As for the test, most explain it as a trial, and Ibn 'Abbas with the majority of exegetes take it to mean who obeys God most. The Prophet, as reported by Ibn 'Umar and cited by al-Zamakhshari, is said to have explained it as the best intellect, the greatest restraint from what God forbids, and the swiftest obedience. Qatada speaks of the most complete intellect, al-Hasan of the greatest renunciation of the world, and al-Dahhak of the greatest gratitude. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi hold that action covers both the heart and the limbs. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di stress that deeds are accepted only when sincere and in line with the Law. The second part of the verse concerns the disbelievers' denial of resurrection, whom they say call the Quran or the announcement of resurrection plain magic. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read 'sorcerer', which then refers to the Prophet. The verse also mentions the delay of punishment until a counted term, which Ibn Kathir takes as a set period, the unbelievers asking for it mockingly.

The commentators explain that God says that if He delays the punishment for the Meccan disbelievers until a counted and fixed term, they will say mockingly and in denial: what is holding it back? God replies that on the day it comes upon them it will not be turned away, and that what they used to mock will surround them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most exegetes, such as Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, understand ummah here as a period or term, though its root sense is a community, since a time is called so because a generation arises within it. Ibn al-Jawzi and others take it to mean the passing of one people and the coming of another. Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur explain that a counted term means a short one, since small quantities are easily counted. On what the punishment is, opinions differ: al-Hasan takes it as the annihilating punishment deferred to the Day of Resurrection, others as the punishment of Badr or the killing of the mockers by Gabriel, and Ibn Kathir as the promised punishment in general. Regarding their words 'what is holding it back', al-Tabari and al-Mawardi see a denial, while al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi also see mocking haste. Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that 'they mock' stands in place of 'they hasten', because their haste was a form of mockery. The grammatical role of the word for day is debated among grammarians, but the meaning is agreed upon.

The commentators explain that the verse describes human nature when circumstances change. If God grants a person a blessing such as health, ease or wealth and then takes it away, he falls into despair and denies the blessing he once had. Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Kathir, al-Jaza'iri and Ibn Sa'di describe a man who does not hope in God's grace and does not endure patiently, while al-Tabari simply says he remains hopeless of God's mercy. As for joy and boasting, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir apply them to the man who, after hardship, says his troubles have gone and then becomes arrogant and vain toward others. Ibn al-Qayyim adds that he forgets the Giver of the blessing.

Most exegetes agree that "man" refers to humankind in general, and that the exception "except those who are patient and do good deeds" includes believers, who endure hardship patiently and give thanks in ease. God grants them forgiveness and a great reward, as al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi state. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan report that some scholars take the verse to refer only to disbelievers, making the exception disconnected, and Ibn 'Atiyya rejects this reading because the quality of disbelief cannot be applied to all people.

Opinions also differ on the person meant. Ibn 'Abbas and others say it was revealed about al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, others about Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya al-Makhzumi, while al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Jawzi read it as referring to mankind. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the meaning stays general while the despair varies among people. Some commentators read "making one taste" as a metaphor for granting, and "ni'ma" as the visible effect of a blessing on the body.

This verse describes a person who, after receiving a blessing following hardship, says that his troubles are gone and becomes exultant and boastful, forgetting to thank God. The commentators broadly agree on the blameworthy nature of this attitude. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain it as ingratitude and pride; Ibn Kathir adds that the person despairs during hardship and forgets past favours. Al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi say the boaster is the one who vaunts himself over believers. Scholars differ on who the word 'man' refers to. Al-Tabari, al-Razi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi take it to mean humankind in general, so the exception of patient believers who do good deeds is a direct exception. Ibn 'Atiyya and others understand it as the disbeliever, which makes the exception disconnected. Ibn Kathir takes the intended person to be the believer who is patient in hardship and grateful in ease, citing the hadith that the believer's affairs are all good. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that joy in itself is not always blameworthy, since the Quran praises joy when it is tied to good. Al-Qurtubi notes different readings of the word for 'joyful'. Al-Sha'rawi stresses that the believer attributes blessings to God, while the one who forgets Him is carried away by vain joy. The patient receive forgiveness and a great reward, which Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri connect with Paradise.

The commentators explain that this verse makes an exception to the general human disposition: a person despairs and is ungrateful when he loses a blessing, and when he receives comfort after hardship he rejoices arrogantly and says that his troubles have gone. The exception concerns those who are patient in adversity and do good deeds, giving thanks in prosperity; they receive forgiveness for their sins and a great reward, which most of them identify as Paradise. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, agree that patience in hardship and gratitude in ease are intended, and that both stem from faith. Al-Tabari holds that the exception is connected, since al-Insan refers to the human species, as in Surat al-Asr; Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi also take this view. By contrast, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, along with those who understand the term as referring only to the disbeliever, read the exception as disjunctive, meaning 'but those who were patient'. A report from Ibn 'Abbas holds that the first description refers to the disbeliever and that those who were patient are the Companions of the Prophet. Al-Razi observes that the word for making someone taste implies the smallest amount of flavour, which shows how quickly the soul changes. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of Suhayb about the wonderful condition of the believer, for whom every matter is good. Ibn Sa'di explains that this is man's natural state unless God guides him to its opposite, and sees in the verse a warning against joy and pride in worldly goods.

This verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ, forbidding him to leave aside any part of what is revealed to him, or to let his heart be constrained by the words of those who say: why was a treasure not sent down to him, or why is no angel sent with him? He is reminded that his duty is only to warn, and that God is guardian over all things. The commentators agree that the verse does not mean he had actually intended to abandon the message; it is an exhortation and a strengthening of his resolve. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir explain that the Quraysh made these demands out of defiance rather than a wish for guidance, and that the Prophet was to be patient as the messengers before him had been. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir add that the constriction of his heart came from their words and conduct. Several authors, including al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and al-Suyuti, relate the occasion of revelation: the Quraysh asked him to omit the insult of their gods, or to bring another Quran, and he was inclined to comply. Regarding the treasure, most understand a great wealth, while al-Razi takes it as means to support his mission and al-Zamakhshari stresses the challenge behind the demand. On the particle la'alla, some read it as hope, others as distancing or as a rebuking question, and most accept it as an exhortation. The word wakil is generally understood as guardian and witness.

This verse reports that the disbelievers claimed the Prophet ﷺ had invented the Quran himself. God commands him to challenge them to produce ten surahs like it, and to call on whomever they can besides God, if they are truthful. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur agree that the likeness meant is in eloquence, fine composition and style, not in the soundness of the content. Al-Zamakhshari compares the challenge to a teacher asking a pupil to copy ten lines and then accepting one line once incapacity is clear. On the order of the challenges, scholars differ: Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes, including Ibn 'Atiyya, hold that the challenge of ten surahs came before the challenge of one surah, while al-Mubarrad holds the reverse, seeing the ten-surah version as a relaxation granted to the opponents. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the word "forged" is a concession, letting the opponents have their way, and does not fix a precise number of surahs. Sayyid Qutb notes that no reliable report fixes the chronological order, and that the demands varied with the objections raised. The commentators agree that the verse closes with an invitation to the unbelievers to submit to Islam once their inability is established, though they differ on who is addressed by "if they do not respond to you".

God tells His Prophet to challenge the disbelievers to produce ten surahs like the Quran, forged by themselves, and to call on whomever they can besides God for help. If those they call do not respond, they should know that the Quran was sent down with God's knowledge, that there is no god but Him, and they should ask themselves whether they will submit. The commentators agree that the polytheists were unable to meet the challenge and that the Quran is from God. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, followed by al-Qurtubi, report that the plural "you" may refer to the Prophet alone out of honour, or to the Prophet together with the believers who also challenged the unbelievers. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan hold that the address may be to the idolaters, whose gods did not answer, so that they come to recognise the truth. Mujahid says that "Will you submit?" is addressed to the Companions of the Prophet, while Ibn 'Abbas holds it refers to the people of Mecca. Al-Razi prefers that the address is to the unbelievers, since the pronoun returns to the nearest mentioned party. Most explain "with the knowledge of God" as with His permission, or with what only God knows, namely an inimitable composition and reports of the unseen. The interrogative "Will you submit?" is an order and an exhortation to embrace Islam, according to all, and for some a call to sincerity and steadfastness. Opinions differ on the precise sense of challenging with ten surahs rather than one.

This verse speaks of those who, by their deeds, seek only the life of this world and its adornments. The commentators explain that God gives them the full reward of their deeds in this world without any reduction, but in the Hereafter they have nothing except the Fire, and their good deeds come to nothing because they were not done for God's sake. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak that such people receive in this life health and provision for their charity, kinship ties or prayers, whereas the believer is rewarded both here and in the afterlife.

The scholars differ on who is meant. Al-Dahhak, followed by al-Nahhas, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi, understood it to refer to unbelievers, relying on the following verse. Mujahid and others included those who perform good deeds to be seen by people, citing the hadith of Abu Hurayra about the three first to be cast into Hell, which Ibn Kathir found relevant. Anas ibn Malik and al-Hasan linked it to Jews and Christians, while al-Razi mentions hypocrites who fought for the spoils. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya note that its wording is general while its intended meaning is more specific.

On the meaning of "wanting", al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain it as aim and intention. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi stress that worldly reward depends on God's will, as the verse in Surat al-Isra' indicates. Al-Qurtubi mentions a view of abrogation transmitted from Ibn Abbas, which others reject in favour of reading the verse as a qualified statement.

This verse states that whoever desires only the present life and its adornment will be given the full reward of his deeds in this world, without any reduction, while in the Hereafter he has nothing but the Fire. What he did there is annulled and vain, because it was not done for the sake of God. The commentators agree on the general meaning: the reward in this world takes the form of health, provision and children, and the 'habt' of deeds means the loss of any reward in the next life. They differ on who is meant. Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes, including al-Shawkani and al-Alusi, take it to refer to disbelievers who deny the Hereafter; Mujahid extends it to show-offs among the Muslims; Anas ibn Malik applies it to Jews and Christians; al-Jubba'i to hypocrites who fought for booty. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan prefer to see the disbelievers as the primary target while allowing others to fall under the rule. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir hold that the person who acts for show is repaid in this world and has no share in the next, citing the hadith of the three who will be first cast into the Fire. Ibn al-Qayyim reports this as Mu'awiya's understanding but argues the verse concerns those who do not seek God's face at all, not believers whose main aim is the Hereafter. Al-Razi lists several views and notes that the conclusion applies to one whose desire is limited to the worldly life. Finally, the reading 'wa-batilan' in the accusative, attributed to 'Asim, is explained by Abu Hayyan and al-Zamakhshari as a direct object of the verb.

This verse contrasts the one who stands on a clear proof from his Lord with the one who wants only the life of this world and its adornment. The commentators agree that it states that whoever stands on that proof believes in the Quran, that whoever rejects it among the various groups is destined for the Fire, that the truth comes from God, and that most people do not believe. On who is meant by 'the one upon a clear proof', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir see the Prophet ﷺ in the main, and Ibn Zayd identifies those who follow him, while al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya lean toward believers among the People of the Book, and al-Zamakhshari reports the same view for 'Abd Allah ibn Salam. For the 'witness' who follows, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrima and al-Dahhak say it is Gabriel, al-Hasan and Qatada say it is the Prophet's tongue, al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl says it is the Quran's inimitability, and al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that Gabriel and the Prophet both conveyed the message, so the two views are close; Ibn Kathir calls the view attributed to 'Ali weak. The 'Book of Moses' is the Torah, which al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi describe as confirming the Quran. On 'the factions', Sa'id ibn Jubayr says they are all religious communities, Qatada says the Jews and Christians, and al-Suddi says the Quraysh. Several commentators, including al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi, note that the prohibition on doubt is addressed to the Prophet but applies to all.

This verse states that no one is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God, such as attributing a partner or a son to Him, or distorting His religion with what He never revealed. These people will be presented before their Lord on the Day of Resurrection to be judged, and the witnesses will declare their lie, a public disgrace for them, accompanied by God's curse and their exclusion from His mercy. The commentators agree that this warning targets those who invent falsehoods about God, but they differ on who the witnesses are. Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, Ibn Jurayj and others identify them as the prophets and messengers; Mujahid, Qatada, al-A'mash and Ibn Kathir identify them as the angels; Qatada in another report, Muqatil and Ibn Juzayy include all the creatures present at the gathering; al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi add that the bodily organs may also serve as witnesses; al-Mawardi reports several other opinions, including prophets, angels, believers and bodies. Most agree that the verse describes barring people from God's path and seeking to make it crooked. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari explain that turning people from the truth means keeping them from the straight way, and that seeking to make it crooked means describing it as deviant. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi note that the repeated pronoun serves to emphasise their disbelief in the Hereafter. As for the statement that their punishment will be doubled, Ibn Kathir and al-Jazairi attribute it to their obstruction of Islam, while al-Razi attributes it to their denial of the Creator and of resurrection along with their misleading of others. Regarding their inability to hear and see, most commentators read it as an expression of their intense aversion to the truth; Ibn Kathir adds that they will be punished for the duties they neglected, and al-Razi holds that the verse does not establish compulsion.

This verse describes those who bar people from God's path, seek to make it crooked, and disbelieve in the Hereafter. The commentators explain that barring means preventing and turning people away from Islam, and that God's path means His religion and law. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi largely agree that it refers to the Quraysh or the polytheists who turned people away from faith. The repetition of the pronoun 'they' is read by most as emphasis on their disbelief in the Hereafter. Al-Suddi and Ibn 'Abbas identify the path with the Prophet himself or with God's religion; Abu Malik says they wanted a religion other than Islam; al-Suddi adds that they sought the Prophet's destruction; 'Ali ibn 'Isa says they distorted the Qur'an by false interpretation. As for 'crooked', al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take it to mean describing the straight way as crooked, or pushing its followers toward apostasy; Ibn al-Qayyim understands it as placing reason above the revealed texts. Several commentators note that the gravest wrong is to invent lies against God, and that witnesses on the Day of Gathering will proclaim the guilt of such people, as Ibn Kathir reports from a hadith about the private conversation between God and the believer.

This verse states that those who turn others away from the path of God and seek to make it crooked cannot escape His power on earth and have no protectors against His punishment, and that their torment will be doubled because they misled both themselves and others. As for the phrase 'they could not hear or see', Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada, followed by most exegetes such as al-Tabari, explain that they could not hear the truth so as to benefit from it, nor see it so as to be guided, because of their clinging to disbelief, although they did possess hearing and sight. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir link the doubled punishment to the misguidance they imposed on their followers. Al-Farra' attributes their inability to a divine misguidance recorded in the Preserved Tablet, al-Zajjaj to their intense hatred of the Prophet, while al-Razi and al-Jubba'i see it as refusal and aversion. Ibn al-Qayyim argues that the verse gives no support to determinists, since it refers to useful hearing. Al-Tabari also mentions the view that a 'bi' is implied, which some grammarians reject. On 'la jarama', al-Khalil, Sibawayh and al-Farra' take it to mean 'certainly', al-Zajjaj as 'it earned them loss', and al-Kisa'i as a negation. All agree that these are the greatest losers in the Hereafter.

This verse states that those who invent lies against God and associate others with Him have lost their own souls and forfeited His mercy, and that what they claimed about their idols and intercessors has vanished and come to nothing. The commentators agree on the core meaning: the true loss is the loss of the self, and these people will bear punishment in the hereafter. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that what they fabricated went astray from them, meaning their falsehoods were annulled, while al-Qurtubi and al-Zamakhshari understand that what they had gained was lost and perished.

The phrase "la jaram" has prompted linguistic debate. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh read it as "truly," al-Farra' as "there is no doubt or escape," and al-Zajjaj connects it to the root meaning "to earn," so that their deeds earned them ruin. Al-Kisa'i renders it as "no hindrance and no prevention," and several grammarians note that the Arabs used this formula in various forms.

The commentators also discuss the "witnesses" (al-ashhad), who are understood as angels, prophets, or all of creation, and they agree that the verse concerns idolaters and disbelievers. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir stress that their punishment will be multiplied because they misled others, and that they were unable to hear and see the truth in this world.

This verse states that those who invented lies against God and lost their own souls through their misguidance will be the greatest losers in the Hereafter, and the phrase « la jaram » is explained in several ways. Al-Tabari renders it as « truly », and explains that their loss lies in exchanging their places in Paradise for the places of the people of the Fire. Al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Jawzi take jaram to mean « earned », so that their own deeds earned them this loss. Sibawayh, al-Khalil and al-Farra' read it as « assuredly » or « without doubt », a phrase that came to function like an oath. Al-Kisa'i reads it as « there is no hindrance », while some grammarians connect it with the idea of cutting off.

Commentators agree that these people lost themselves by preferring idolatry to the worship of God, and that the gods in whom they trusted vanished from them. Ibn Kathir stresses that they traded the ranks of Paradise for the descent into Hell, and al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi hold that their loss exceeds every other. Al-Razi notes that they cannot escape God, while al-Zamakhshari adds that they could not escape him in this world either.

Opinions differ on the deafness and blindness mentioned in the verse. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as blindness to the truth and deafness to it, al-Razi speaks of a deaf heart and a blind insight, and al-Jubba'i reads it as refusal and aversion. On the verb « akhbatu », Ibn al-Jawzi reports the meanings of fearing, turning back to God, being at peace, or humbling oneself, which are close to one another.

This verse states that those who believe, do righteous deeds and humble themselves before their Lord are the companions of the Garden, where they will remain forever. The commentators agree that the verb akhbata means to submit, to be humble and to find peace in God, and that its root refers to low, level ground. Al-Tabari reports the different explanations: Ibn 'Abbas took it to mean fear, Mujahid tranquility, Qatada returning in repentance to God, and Muqatil sincerity, while al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba understood humility and reverence. Al-Tabari judges these meanings to be close to one another, since returning to God arises from fear and tranquility arises from humility.

Al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi cite the same meanings as separate opinions. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Su'ud gloss the word as settling and submitting, linking it to the image of low ground. Al-Razi distinguishes two readings: if it means tranquility, the heart is at rest while worshipping; if it means fear, the believer dreads falling short in his deeds. Ibn al-Qayyim observes that all these definitions turn around two axes, humility and serenity in God.

The preposition ila is explained by al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur as meaning li, or as directing one's submission toward God. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the verse answers the description of the ruin of the disbelievers by presenting the happy end of the believers. Al-Alusi reads it as describing those who reach faith through hearing and reflecting on the signs.

In this verse God draws a comparison between two groups: the disbelievers and the believers. The disbeliever is likened to the blind and the deaf, and the believer to the one who sees and the one who hears. The commentators explain that the disbeliever does not see the truth so as to follow it, nor hear God's call so as to be guided by it, and so remains lost and bewildered in his error, while the believer has perceived God's proofs, acknowledged them and obeyed His call. Al-Tabari, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, as well as Ibn Kathir, agree that the blind and the deaf stand for the disbeliever and the seeing and hearing stand for the believer. On the grammar, opinions differ. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Atiyya hold that each group is compared to two images, one for blindness and one for deafness, with the conjunction joining two distinct figures. Al-Tabari, followed by Ibn al-Jawzi, holds instead that the conjunction links two attributes of a single figure, so that the blind-deaf and the seeing-hearing each form one example. Al-Razi relates the comparison to the human being made of body and soul, the heart of the ignorant being blind and deaf as the body would be without its senses. The commentators also note that the closing question, 'Will you not then remember?', calls for reflection and awareness, and that the denial of equality between the two groups expresses the vast gap separating them.

This verse reports that God sent Noah to his people to warn them clearly of the punishment that would come if they associated others with God, commanding them to worship God alone and warning them of the painful day. The commentators agree that the nadhir is the one who warns against the consequences of disbelief, and that the mubin is the one who makes his message plain. They read this as the call to monotheism at the core of Noah's mission. Al-Tabari holds that the two readings, with kasra and with fatha on the hamza of inni, are equivalent in meaning: the kasra implies an implied verb of saying, while the fatha implies that the sending was accompanied by this message, a view also followed by Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi explain that attributing pain to the day is a metonymy, since the pain belongs to the one punished, as one says his day is fasting. The following verses record the objections of the notables of his people, who doubted that a human could be a messenger, criticised that only the lowly followed him, and considered their adherence a hasty opinion. Al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya report several possible meanings of bady al-ra'y, while Ibn Kathir holds that the phrase is not a reproach, since manifest truth needs no long deliberation. Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi understand the arādhil as people of low station and humble trades.

This verse states the content of Noah's mission to his people: he is a clear warner sent to make plain what he was entrusted with. The commentators agree that the heart of his message is to worship God alone and to abandon the worship of idols and false gods, and that he fears for them the punishment of a painful day if they persist in associating others with God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take the prohibition to be against polytheism, with worship meaning here the affirmation of God's oneness. All agree that describing the day as painful is a figurative attribution, since the pain is really felt by those punished, and they give the example of a day that is said to fast. On recitation, readers differed over whether the hamza of inni is vowelled with a kasra or a fatha. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read it with a fatha, meaning that he was sent with the message that, while the others read it with a kasra, implying a verb of saying. Al-Tabari judges both readings equally correct in meaning. Ibn 'Atiyya notes the grammatical difference and mentions a shift from third to second person discussed by Abu 'Ali. Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan consider that the particle can be either explanatory or a complement. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the warning is justified to soften its impact on listeners who find it hard to hear.

This verse records the reply of the chiefs of Noah's people to his call. They say he is only a human like them, with no distinction that would make him fit for prophethood, that those who followed him are their lowest, meaning people of despised trades, that no notable has followed him, and that they followed him bādi al-ra'y, meaning at first glance, without deep reflection. The commentators agree that al-mala' means the notables and al-arādhil means people of low standing, but they differ on bādi al-ra'y: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi take it as the apparent opinion or the first thought, al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari say these people did not reflect enough, and Mujahid and Abu Hayyan take it as what is visible to the eye. Al-Tabari and al-Sam'ani report both readings, with and without the hamza, and their meanings. Al-Zamakhshari understands that the unbelievers judged the truth by the humble status of its followers, while Ibn 'Atiyya sees in it only an implied claim that they themselves deserved prophethood. Ibn 'Abbas explains fadl as physical stature, Muqatil as wealth and power, and al-Kalbi reads nazunnukum as certainty, whereas Muqatil reads it as supposition. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim stress that the modest condition of the believers does not discredit the truth, and that differences of rank among people do not cancel the prophetic mission. The general sense is that the opponents measured the message by wealth and rank, which the commentators regard as a mistake.

In this verse Noah addresses his people: tell me, if I have a clear proof from my Lord and He has given me mercy, meaning prophethood and guidance, yet it has been hidden from your sight, shall I force it upon you when you dislike it? The commentators explain that the proof is clear in itself and that the blindness comes from the people's refusal and stubbornness. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that mercy refers to prophethood or guidance, and that the proof refers to the argument or the miracle. The reading of the verb varies: with a short mim and an open ayn it means that you became blind to it; with a doubled mim it means that it was concealed. Al-Tabari prefers the second reading because it links the mercy to God. Al-Zamakhshari treats the verb as a metaphor: the proof, which should give sight, has become blind and no longer guides. He reports that Ubayy's reading, which makes God the subject, means that God left them to their stubbornness, and that this leaving became the blinding; Abu Hayyan criticises this Mu'tazilite-style reading. Several scholars, including al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and Ibn Sa'di, take the question as a denial: Noah has no power to compel them. Qatada even says that had he been able, he would have done so. Al-Qasimi reads the verse as an invitation to reflect, and al-Sha'rawi stresses that faith belongs to the heart and free choice, citing that there is no compulsion in religion. The grammatical points on the vowel of the first mim and on the joining of the two pronouns are discussed by Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Zamakhshari, but the general meaning remains the same: the truth is clear, and compulsion is not the intended means.

This passage relates Noah's words to his people: he asks them for no wealth in return for calling them to the worship of God alone, since his reward rests with God, and he cannot drive away the believers who follow him, because they will meet their Lord, who will judge and reward them. He tells them that asking him to do so shows their ignorance. The commentators agree that the 'lowly' are the poor believers, and that Noah's people wanted them removed so the notables would not have to sit with them. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir say this was a request from the chiefs, and Ibn Kathir compares it to the Quraysh's demand made to the Prophet, peace be upon him. Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir explain 'the apparent opinion' as following without reflection, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi see the ignorance as ignorance of meeting God or of these believers' standing before Him. On 'we would compel you to accept it', most take it as compelling acceptance of guidance, and Ibn Atiyya discusses the reading of the vowel. Al-Razi explains that Noah's argument is that the proof was obscured for his people without any fault in the proof itself. Views differ on 'meeting their Lord': some take it as reward in the afterlife, others as being called to account. Al-Zamakhshari reads misguidance as abandonment after obstinacy, while Abu Hayyan notes it may also mean perdition.

Noah tells his people that if he drove away the believers who followed him, no one could shield him from God's punishment, and he urges them to reflect. The commentators agree that the 'driving away' refers to pushing aside the poor and weak believers whom the people wanted removed, and that the question is a rhetorical rebuke meant to awaken their minds. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain it as who would protect him from God's punishment if he sent them away, while al-Zamakhshari reports that the notables wanted the believers removed so as not to be on equal footing with them. Al-Tabari treats such expulsion as an injustice to monotheists. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi point out that Noah is answering their demand by stating that the faith and fate of these men belong to God, and that 'they will meet their Lord' may be a mark of honour for them or a warning against their complaint before God. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud hold that driving them away is a wrong that brings divine wrath, whereas the Jalalayn and the Muyassar simply stress that no one can protect against God. Al-Tabari links the verse to what precedes it: Noah asks no wealth of them, claims no treasures of God, and does not say he is an angel. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the verb nasara here means to deliver from punishment and records the readings of tadhakkarun, with or without doubling.

This verse records Noah telling his people that he does not possess the treasures of God, meaning His provision and wealth, that he does not know the unseen, and that he is not an angel but a human messenger. The commentators read it as a reply to the objections of his people, who argued that only the lowly followed him and that he had no advantage over them. Noah answers that true superiority lies in revelation and mercy, not in wealth, rank or outward appearance. Ibn 'Abbas explains the treasures as mercy, while al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand them as wealth or hidden knowledge. Al-Zamakhshari links the denial of knowing the unseen to the preceding clause, and does not take it as a claim Noah makes. Most exegetes hold that Noah does not judge the poor believers whom his people despise, since God knows what is in their hearts; if they are sincere, they will be rewarded. Ibn Kathir adds that declaring them deprived of good after their faith would be an injustice. Al-Razi uses the verse in the debate over whether angels surpass prophets, whereas Ibn 'Ashur and al-Biqa'i see it mainly as a rebuttal of objections. Al-Sha'rawi notes that the address shifts to the third person when speaking of "those your eyes despise", so Noah does not address them directly. All agree that Noah claims nothing false and that God alone knows the hearts.

This verse reports the words of Noah's people after a long dispute with him: you have argued with us and argued at length, so bring us what you threaten us with, if you are truthful. The commentators explain that they mean he will not be able to bring about what he threatens, and that their words deny his warning. Most agree that jidal means a contentious debate aimed at prevailing, derived from the sense of tightly twisting. Mujahid and Ibn Abbas equate it with mira' (wrangling), and Ibn Abbas read the verb as jadalana, meaning the debate itself. Al-Sam'ani distinguishes praiseworthy debate that seeks to establish the truth from blameworthy wrangling that continues after the truth has appeared. Ibn Atiyya holds that debating a hostile opponent is praiseworthy when one hopes to guide him to faith.

Most exegetes take the punishment to mean the immediate chastisement, while some link it to the painful day that Noah had warned of. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the phrase "if you are truthful" concerns the truthfulness of his prophethood and his threat. According to the commentators, Noah replies that God alone brings the punishment if He wills, that they cannot escape Him, and that his counsel will not benefit them if God wishes to lead them astray. They differ on the meaning of "lead astray": for Ibn Abbas and al-Tabari it means misguiding them, while others take it to mean destroying them. Ibn Kathir notes that the passage refutes the Mu'tazila, and al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi read it as evidence against their doctrine of divine will.

Noah tells his people that the punishment is not in his hands but in God's: He will bring it when He wills, and they cannot escape it. Most commentators explain the phrase "if He wills" as meaning that God brings the punishment sooner or later according to His wisdom, as Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud put it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it rather as meaning that the one who punishes them and hastens it is God, whom nothing can overpower. All agree that Noah is thereby clearing himself of responsibility for the punishment they were demanding. As for the phrase "my counsel will not benefit you", al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi explain it as their refusal to accept advice, and as the fact that if God wills to lead them astray, no counsel will help them. The meaning of "lead astray" divides the scholars: Ibn 'Abbas and al-Tabari take it as misguidance, al-Zamakhshari explains it as leaving a disbeliever to persist in his stubbornness, while others, reported by Ibn 'Atiyya, take it to mean ruin or destruction. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that this reading removes the Mu'tazilite argument. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir focus on the closing words: to Him you will return.

This passage from the story of Noah states that his counsel will not benefit his people if God has willed to lead them astray, that is, to leave them in error because of their stubbornness. The commentators report that Noah gives this answer to their impatience and their challenge, reminding them that punishment belongs to God alone, who will bring it when He wills, and that they cannot escape it. Most commentators, such as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan, understand the verb yughwiyakum as "to lead astray". Al-Tabari also gives the sense of "to destroy", relying on Arab usage in which a suckling camel that has gorged on milk and died is said to have gone astray. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya note that this wording may seem to attribute to God the creation of error, which the Mu'tazilites reject, while the Sunni scholars see in it proof that the divine will is executed. Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi also observe that the verse contains two chained conditions whose answer is implied, and that the second condition governs the first. For most of them, the closing words, "He is your Lord, and to Him you will be returned", remind the listeners that God disposes of His creation and that the return will be to Him, which amounts to a warning. Sayyid Qutb stresses that the messenger fulfils his duty of delivery to the last moment, and that if ruin comes, it comes through the people's own choice.

The verse reports that some people claim the Prophet invented this account, or that Noah invented it, and God commands him to reply that if he had forged it, the sin would fall on him alone, and that he is innocent of the crimes his opponents commit by making this accusation. The commentators explain that ijram means earning a sin or misdeed, and they note the reading ajrami with an open hamza as the plural of jurm. The sense is therefore: if I forged it, the penalty for my offence is mine, and you will answer for your rejection. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan give this meaning and cite the line of verse about the word jarama. Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and the Jalalayn take the words to address the Prophet and the Quraysh, while al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Sa'di connect them to Noah's story. Ibn 'Ashur sees a parenthetical sentence that confirms what came earlier in the surah, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi read it as a disavowal aimed at those who despair of being persuaded. Al-Sha'rawi points out that the verse leaves the innocence of the opponents unstated, a figure called ihtibak, and al-Qasimi follows a similar reading. Sayyid Qutb sees it as an interruption in the narrative answering the charge of invention, and the commentators agree that each person bears the responsibility for his own deeds.

The verse tells Noah, after a very long period of preaching, that none of his people will believe except those who already have, and it bids him not to grieve over what they do. The commentators agree on the core meaning: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, citing Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Abbas, explain that 'fa-la tabta'is' means 'do not grieve', with ibti'as denoting grief together with humiliation. Al-Tabari adds that this revelation came after Noah had prayed against the unbelievers, asking God to leave none of them on the earth. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read the verse as a declaration of despair regarding their faith, and as a statement that their drowning has already been decreed and cannot be averted. Ibn Atiyya concludes that this verse is what took away Noah's hope in his people. Al-Razi reports a dispute on predestination: the Ash'arites take the verse as proof that God's foreknowledge of disbelief does not contradict the duty to believe, while the Mu'tazilites hold that destroying a people among whom some future believer might arise is not permitted. On the wording, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya stress the sense of 'until'-style exclusion, and Ibn Ashur explains that the emphatic particle expresses total and lasting negation. The Jalalayn and al-Qasimi see the verse simply as God's word of reassurance to Noah, and Ibn Sa'di sees it as a consolation for Noah in the face of unbelief. Most of the commentators also discuss the building of the ark that follows, and they differ on its dimensions and the number of believers who boarded it.

God commands Noah to build the ark under His watchful eye and by His revelation, and forbids him to plead with Him for the wrongdoers among his people, since they are already condemned to drown. The commentators agree that "before Our eyes" means under Our protection and care, and that the plural expresses majesty rather than number. Mujahid and Qatada read it as divine watchfulness, al-Tabari reports the same, while Muqatil takes it as divine knowledge and others as the angels appointed to guard him. Most take the revelation to be God's instruction in how to build the vessel, and several report on the authority of Ibn Abbas that Noah did not know the craft and was told to shape it like a bird's breast. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir understand the prohibition as a ban on asking for the punishment to be delayed. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy add that the "wrongdoers" could mean his wife and son, a view Ibn Atiyya considers weak. When the notables mock him while he builds, Noah replies that they will in turn be mocked. The scholars differ on what the mockery means: some see it as ridicule of his foolishness, while al-Tabari and Ibn Juzayy see the reply as a future mockery in the afterlife. Accounts of the ark's dimensions vary widely, and most commentators decline to fix a precise measure.

This verse describes Noah building the ark under God's command and watchful eye. Whenever chiefs of his people passed by, they mocked him for his work. He answered that if they mock him now, he will mock them later, when the punishment comes, and warns that they will soon know who will suffer a humiliating punishment and a lasting torment. Commentators explain the mockery in several ways: people saw him building a ship far from water, or had never known ships before, or found it absurd that he predicted a flood with no sign of one. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi mainly read the mockery as an expression of ignorance and ridicule, with the reply as a mirror of their words. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya take the coming mockery as drowning in this world and burning in the next. Al-Tabari sees it as mockery in the hereafter. The details of the ark's size, the time it took to build and its decks differ widely, and several scholars, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi, consider them unreliable or unhelpful; al-Baghawi and al-Alusi trace many of them to Israelite narrations. Al-Razi says such matters are of no real benefit. Many commentators hold that Noah's mockery of his people is a rhetorical reply in kind, since real mockery would not suit a prophet.

This verse records Noah's reply to his people, who mocked him while he was building the ark: you will soon learn who will receive a punishment that humiliates him in this world, and upon whom a lasting punishment will descend. The commentators agree that the humiliating punishment is the flood and the lasting punishment is that of the Hereafter, and that the warning is addressed to Noah's mockers. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that 'yahillu' means 'descends' or 'becomes due', like a debt whose term has come and from which there is no escape. Al-Tabari takes 'fara al-tannur' to mean that water gushed from the surface of the earth, or from the bread oven, and he prefers the second sense because it is the most familiar usage in Arabic. Other opinions, reported by Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, mention the rising of dawn, the mosque of Kufa, or a spring in the Jazira. On the reason for the mockery, al-Razi and al-Baydawi give several explanations: they saw him building a ship far from any water, they had never seen a ship, or they doubted that the threat would be fulfilled after so long a delay. The number of believers who boarded with Noah varies among the scholars, from seven or eight to ten, seventy-eight and eighty; al-Tabari concludes that no definite number can be fixed. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the comparison 'as you mock' concerns the cause of the mockery, with the believers mocking from knowledge of the disbelievers' ignorance. Al-Alusi and Ibn 'Atiyya understand the mockery as ridicule grounded in the accusation of ignorance.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the moment when God's command to flood arrives after Noah has built the ark. The water gushes forth as the sign that destruction has begun, and Noah is told to take aboard a pair of every kind of creature, male and female, along with his family and those who believed, except those against whom the word has already gone forth, such as his son and his wife. The small number of believers is emphasised. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the water burst from the oven used for baking, which served as a sign to Noah for the time of boarding, while Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, al-Zuhri and Ibn Uyayna say that the tannur means the surface of the earth, a usage known among the Arabs. Ali ibn Abi Talib takes it to mean the dawn, and al-Sha'bi and Mujahid place the oven in Kufa. Al-Razi favours the literal sense of the word, whereas al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur read it as an image of the extreme severity of the moment. On the number of believers, Ibn Abbas says eighty people, Qatada eight, Ibn Ishaq ten and al-A'mash seven. Al-Tabari declines to fix a figure without an authentic text, and Ibn Kathir holds that Noah's wife was not on board. Al-Zamakhshari uses this verse to explain that the exception regarding the family refers to those already condemned for their disbelief.

The commentators explain that Noah told those he had been commanded to carry with him to board the ship, saying: embark in it in the name of God; its sailing and its anchoring are by His will. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand that God's name accompanies both the departure and the arrival, and that the closing words, "indeed my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful", mean that He pardons those who repent and shows mercy to His servants. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi conclude from this that invoking God's name when boarding is recommended, and Ibn Kathir cites a hadith on the matter while noting the weakness of its chain. On recitation, al-Tabari prefers opening the mim in "majraha" and closing it in "mursaha", while most readers vowel both with a damma; al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan set out the readings and their grammatical implications. The grammatical analysis is also debated: the phrase may form one sentence or two, with "in the name of God" possibly describing the act of boarding. Al-Razi observes that one should begin any task by mentioning God's name, and that deliverance comes from God rather than from the ship alone. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi explain that God's mercy and forgiveness, not the merit of the passengers, are the cause of their rescue. According to al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, the ship set sail in Rajab and came to rest on al-Judi on the day of 'Ashura, though the commentators differ on some details of this chronology.

The verse describes the ark sailing with Noah and those with him through waves as high as mountains, then Noah calls out to his son, who was apart from them, urging him to board and not to join the disbelievers. The commentators agree that the word "mawj" refers to the water that rises when stirred by strong winds, and that the comparison with mountains concerns size and height. On the son, most hold that he was Noah's own son and an unbeliever; Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrima and al-Dahhak name him Kan'an. Al-Hasan, Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj argue instead that he was the son of Noah's wife and not his offspring, a view that Ibn Kathir and al-Razi reject. As for the phrase "no protector today from Allah's command, except him on whom He has mercy", al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read it as meaning that no one can shield from Allah's punishment except Allah Himself. Others, such as al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya, read "'asim" as "ma'sum" (protected), making the exception a connected one. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi suggest the ark moved through the waves before the flood fully covered the land, a view some find weak, while al-Qurtubi reports the waters rising some fifteen cubits above the mountains.

This passage recounts that Noah called out to his son, who had kept apart, urging him to board the ark with him and not to remain with the disbelievers. The son replied that he would take refuge on a mountain that would protect him from the water. Noah answered that there is no protector today from the command of God, meaning His punishment and the flood, except for the one on whom He has mercy. The commentators differ on the grammar of "man" and the meaning of "protector". Al-Tabari takes it as the nominative, meaning that none saves except the Merciful, who is God, and he reports the views of the grammarians of Kufa and Basra, which he finds less consistent with the most eloquent usage. Al-Zajjaj, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Kathir and Muqatil take the exception as disjunctive: rather, the one God has mercy upon is the one preserved. Al-Mawardi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud understand the protected place to be the ark, where the believers are. Al-Zamakhshari lists several possibilities, and al-Baydawi notes several as well. The commentators also disagree about the son. Most, including Ibn Abbas, Ibn Kathir and largely al-Razi, take him to be Noah's own son, named Kan'an or Yam. Al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibn Jurayj and Abu Ja'far al-Baqir say he was the son of his wife. The passage ends with the wave coming between father and son, and the son was among those drowned.

This verse describes the end of the Flood: the earth is commanded to swallow the water on its surface, the sky to stop raining, the waters recede, God's decree is fulfilled by the destruction of the disbelievers and the salvation of the believers, the Ark comes to rest on Mount al-Judi, and then a curse is pronounced against the wrongdoing people, that they be removed far away. The commentators agree on the meaning of the key terms: "ablaʿi" means to absorb or drink, "aqliʿi" means to stop raining, and "ghiḍa" means that the water subsided and sank into the ground. Most place al-Judi in the region of Mosul or al-Jazira, though al-Zajjaj places it near Amid and others in Syria. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi report that the Ark settled on the day of Ashura and that Noah and his companions fasted in gratitude, while noting that these reports are of disputed reliability. On the address to earth and sky, most see a metaphor for God's absolute power, whereas al-Razi allows that God may give them a kind of understanding. Scholars differ over who speaks the curse "bu'dan": al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take it as God's words, while al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari allow that it may be Noah and the believers. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan analysed the eloquence of the verse at length, considering it a peak of Quranic expression.

Nuh calls upon his Lord about his son, relying on God's promise to save his family and affirming that the promise is true and that God is the wisest of judges. The reply tells him that this son is not among his family who were promised salvation, because his conduct is not righteous, and forbids him to ask about what he has no knowledge of. The commentators agree that true kinship is based on faith and good deeds rather than blood alone, that Nuh did not know his son's real state, and that his request came from paternal compassion. The identity of the son, however, is disputed. Ibn 'Abbas, Ikrima, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, Ibn Kathir and most scholars, including al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, hold that he was Nuh's biological son, and understand the verse as denying that he belonged to his family in religion. Al-Hasan al-Basri, Mujahid, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Ibn Jurayj and Abu Ja'far al-Baqir argue that he was born from another union or was the son of the wife, citing the verse about betrayal. Many scholars reject this view as incompatible with the honour of prophets' wives. Regarding the recitation of the phrase 'innahu 'amalun ghayru salih, most readers use the nominative form, while al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read the verb form 'amila with ghayra, meaning he committed disbelief and denial. Al-Razi judges Nuh's act to be an error of judgment rather than a grave sin, while az-Zamakhshari sees a rebuke for this confusion.

The commentators explain that Noah asked God to save his son, and God replied that this son was not among the household He had promised to save, because his deed was not righteous, meaning because of his disbelief and his opposition to his father's faith; God then forbade him to ask about what he had no knowledge of and admonished him lest he be among the ignorant. Many of them agree that the criterion of belonging to the household is kinship in faith rather than kinship by blood, as held by Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi stress that righteousness is the basis of salvation. The disagreement concerns the son's descent: al-Hasan, Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj hold that he was not Noah's biological son but was born on his bed, relying on this verse and other arguments, whereas Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, al-Dahhak, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and most exegetes say he was his son, and al-Tabari judges this more correct since God calls him his son; Ibn Abbas, as cited by Ibn Kathir, held that a prophet's wife never committed adultery. The readers also differ: al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read the verb 'amila, while the majority read the noun 'amalun, and scholars debate whether the pronoun refers to the request or to the son. On the phrase 'fala tas'alni ma laysa laka bihi 'ilm', some see it as an attribution of the son to Noah, others as a request to save an unbeliever; al-Razi judges Noah erred in his judgment without committing a grave sin, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya see a rebuke for neglecting what was better.

This verse records Noah's prayer in which he seeks refuge with his Lord from asking about something he has no knowledge of, and asks for forgiveness and mercy so that he will not be among the losers. The commentators read it as Noah's repentance for his request to save his son. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi agree that losing means being deprived of one's own good and perishing. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the prohibition concerns a future request for something whose soundness one does not know, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi restrict it to an insistent request about matters whose wisdom is hidden, excluding questions asked to learn or be guided. On the identity of the son, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ikrima and the majority hold that he was Noah's own son but disbelieving in faith and conduct. Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj and al-Baqir hold that he was the son of his wife from another union, born on a different bed. Ibn Kathir favours the first view as the correct one. Al-Razi argues that Noah judged by ijtihad, so his lapse was an error of judgment rather than a grave sin. Al-Sha'rawi notes that Noah could not suppress his wish, so he asked God to preserve him from such requests, as a sign of complete submission.

This verse recounts what was said to Noah as he came down from the ark: that he should descend in peace and security from God, and that blessings should rest upon him and upon the communities that would arise from those who were with him. The commentators explain that the blessed communities are the believers among his descendants until the Day of Resurrection, as Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi reports: every believing man and woman enters this peace until the Last Day, while every disbeliever enters the enjoyment and the punishment. The exegetes agree that blessing means the lasting increase of goodness, and that after the Flood Noah became the father of the surviving humanity. Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi state that all mankind descends from him, and al-Baghawi cites the verse about his descendants being the ones who remain to say that he was a second Adam. As for the communities given a brief enjoyment of worldly life, most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, take them to be disbelievers from his line, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan read the word 'min' as indicating origin, so that these communities arise from those who were with him and include both believers and unbelievers. Al-Mawardi and al-Wahidi likewise take them as disbelievers. Some, including al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi, mention that they may be the peoples of Hud, Salih, Lot and Shu'ayb. Al-Tabari reports that al-Hasan, when reciting this passage, said that God saved Noah and those who believed, while those who enjoyed worldly life perished.

This verse states that the story of Noah, with all its details, belongs to the news of the unseen, which neither the Prophet ﷺ nor his people knew before, and that God revealed it to him. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that he received it in its true form, not through human teaching, which proves the truth of the revelation. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take "that" to refer to the story of Noah, while Ibn Juzayy and al-Alusi also take it to refer to the verses of the Quran; Ibn al-Jawzi considers both meanings possible. As for "nor your people", al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that despite their numbers they had not heard of it, let alone any individual among them. Al-Razi adds that the flood was known in outline, but its details were not.

The commentators agree that the command to be patient is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ in the face of rejection and persecution, as Noah was patient, and that the good end, in this world through victory and in the next through success, belongs to the God-fearing. Al-Tabari defines them as those who avoid shirk and sins. Al-Razi stresses that the story consoles the Prophet and shows that patience leads to victory, and Ibn Kathir recalls that God supports his messengers as he did before.

Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that the story holds lessons both for believers and for disbelievers, and that the good end is reserved for piety. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the verse combines gratitude, exhortation and consolation, and that the command to patience is justified by the fact that the end belongs to the pious.

This verse tells that God sent Hud, a man from the tribe of 'Ad, to his own people. He called them to worship God alone and to abandon any other deity, and he described their worship of idols as a lie fabricated against God. Commentators such as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi agree that the word "brother" means that Hud was of their lineage, not of their faith, and that "you are only liars" means that they attribute partners to God by taking idols as such. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi note that Hud asked no payment from his people and expected his reward from God alone, which shows the sincerity of his advice, a point also developed by Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari.

Opinions differ on the meaning of the seeking of forgiveness and the repentance that follow. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi take it as a call first to faith in God and then to turning away from sins, since repentance from wrongdoing is valid only after belief, as al-Zamakhshari also explains. As for the promise of abundant rain and added strength, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd understood bodily vigour, al-Dahhak prosperity added to prosperity, while Ikrima and Ibn 'Abbas understood offspring. Ibn 'Atiyya recalls that this people lived by fields and gardens and so greatly needed water, and several commentators report that God had withheld rain for three years.

The commentators do not choose between these readings; they present them side by side without ruling in favour of one.

This verse records Hud's words to his people, 'Ad: I ask you for no payment for my message; my reward rests only with the One who created me. Will you not then use your reason? The commentators generally understand the 'wage' as a material gain, and see in these words a renunciation of any personal benefit so that the advice remains pure and free from suspicion. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan and al-Baydawi explain its purpose as removing accusation and freeing the counsel from worldly desire, and al-Zamakhshari notes that every messenger said this to his people. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di take the rejected wage to be earthly payment, with the hoped-for reward coming from God alone. Al-Razi adds that a call to God purified of worldly greed has stronger effect on the heart. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya take 'fatara' to mean creating and originating, and al-Qurtubi specifies that fitra is the beginning of creation. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan hold that the pronoun in 'upon it' refers to the call to God. As for 'will you not reason', al-Razi and al-Nasafi read it as an invitation to consider the sincerity of the counsel, while Abu al-Su'ud reads it as a general rebuke of heedlessness and ignorance. All agree on the core meaning: the verse affirms the sincerity of the call and God's sole right to reward. The differences concern mainly the interpretation of particular terms rather than the central message.

In this verse Hud urges his people to seek forgiveness from their Lord and then turn back to Him in repentance. In return, God will send abundant, repeated rain upon them and add strength to their strength, provided they do not turn away from the message as guilty people. Most commentators agree that istighfar here means faith in God and the abandonment of idolatry; al-Tabari, al-Nasafi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take this view, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that repentance is valid only after faith, and Ibn 'Atiyya adds that it requires a firm resolve not to return to the sin.

On the word midrar, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd understand it as rain that follows continuously, while Harun al-Taymi takes it as rain in its proper season and al-Mawardi also suggests it means rain that brings blessing. On the increase of strength, opinions differ: Mujahid and Ibn Zayd understand bodily vigour, al-Dahhak fertility, Ikrima the children of one's children, and Ibn 'Abbas, through Abu Salih, children and grandchildren. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi recall that this people was proud of its might and wealth, so the promise addressed that pride. Al-Mawardi and al-Baydawi also mention strength of faith added to strength of body.

The commentators note that the land had suffered drought for three years, which explains the appeal of the promise of rain, and Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as a warning against returning to idolatry.

This verse records the reply of Hud's people when he called them to worship God alone and abandon the idols. They said he had brought them no clear proof that would compel belief, that they would not give up their gods merely on his word, and that they would not believe him. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Atiyya, agree that this is a rejection of prophethood and a clinging to an inherited cult, and that their claim of having received no proof is a lie and a denial, since Hud had in fact brought signs, though the verse does not specify them. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi explain that the phrase "on your word" may indicate cause or circumstance, meaning they would not abandon their gods as a result of his words. Ibn Juzayy takes "proof" to mean a miracle that would compel faith. Al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya note that prophets have miracles even when these are not named for us. As for their charge that a god had afflicted him with madness after he insulted their idols, most commentators, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir among them, read it as an accusation of insanity, while Ibn Ashur finds the argument poorly reasoned. Hud then disowned the idols and challenged his people to plot against him without delay, declaring his trust in God, who holds every creature by its forelock and whose path is straight. The commentators draw from this that one man stood before a powerful and arrogant people in complete confidence in God's support, and that their obstinacy and denial were the cause of their refusal to believe.

This passage recounts the reply of Hud's people. They tell him that he has brought no proof that would oblige them to believe, that they will not abandon their gods on his word alone, and that they do not believe him. They add that the only explanation they can see for his words is that one of their gods has struck him with madness for insulting it and forbidding them to worship it.
