Hud answers that he calls God to witness his innocence of the idols and partners they associate with Him, calls them to witness it too, and challenges them to scheme against him together with their gods without delay, for he relies on God, his Lord and theirs, who holds every creature by its forelock and who is on a straight path. The commentators, from al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir to al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, explain that 'i'tarak' means 'has struck' or 'has seized you', that 'bi-su'' means madness or derangement, and that these words were ignorant and stubborn. They agree that Hud was confident in God's protection. They differ on the meaning of 'forelock': al-Farra' takes it to mean owner and one who has power, al-Qutaybi takes it to mean one who subdues, and Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Jawzi recall that the Arabs cut the forelock of a captive to mark his subjection, a custom the Qur'an uses in terms they would understand. Al-Zamakhshari observes that Hud calls his people to witness in the imperative to show contempt for them, while calling God to witness in the declarative form to honour Him. Al-Razi and al-Baghawi note that the indefinite 'su'' may indicate a slight or a serious harm. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi see in this scene, where one man defies an entire nation and is not harmed, a sign of Hud's prophethood.

This passage from Surah Hud recounts what the people of 'Ad said to their prophet Hud when they rejected his miracle and refused to abandon the worship of their idols. They claimed that one of their gods had struck him with madness because he insulted them and forbade their worship. Hud answered that he calls God to witness and calls them to witness that he disowns what they associate with Him, and then he challenged them to plot against him all together without giving him any respite. He said that his trust is in God, his Lord and theirs, and that every creature is held by its forelock, meaning it is under His power, and that his Lord is on a straight path. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that "i'taraka" means "has struck you", and that the challenge is a sign of Hud's truthfulness, since he stood alone before a powerful people who wanted to kill him. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi compare this defiance to Noah's words to his people in Surah Yunus. For al-Zamakhshari, the call to bear witness is a mockery rather than a real testimony, whereas al-Razi sees it as a way of establishing the proof against them. Several commentators explain the image of holding by the forelock as a sign of power and domination, recalling that the Arabs would cut the forelock of a prisoner they freed as a mark of his defeat. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi add that "straight path" means that God does not wrong anyone. The commentators largely agree, with differences mainly over the meaning of certain words and the nature of the witness being called.

Hud tells his people that he has put his trust in God, his Lord and theirs, and that every creature that walks the earth is under His control, held by its forelock. The commentators agree that the image of seizing the forelock expresses complete power and mastery, and al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain that the Arabs used this expression for a person who is humbled, since they would shave the forelock of a captive to mark his submission. On the closing phrase, "my Lord is on a straight path", al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, following Mujahid, understand it as "on the truth", while al-Razi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir stress that God, though all-powerful, never wrongs anyone and rewards the good and the wicked according to their deeds. Al-Mawardi and al-Wahidi add that the way is the straight religion Hud was sent with, or a firm plan, and al-Baghawi notes that some read an implied verb, meaning that the Lord guides or urges people onto the straight path. Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes between the forelock verse as affirming God's dominion and the straight-path phrase as affirming the justice and wisdom of His acts, and he rejects the view that the verse only means God is never escaped. Al-Razi and Ibn Ashur see the verse as a proof of prophethood, since a lone messenger who entrusts himself to God can face a powerful people without fear. Most commentators thus agree on the reading of the verse as an assertion of God's sovereignty joined to His justice.

Hud tells his people that if they turn away from his call to worship God alone and abandon the idols, he has delivered his message and the proof stands against them. God will destroy them and replace them with a people more obedient to Him. The commentators agree that the verb tawallaw originally reads tatawallaw, with one of the two taa's dropped, and means turning away from faith. On the phrase 'I have conveyed to you', al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir understand it as the establishment of the proof against them, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan stress that Hud is not blamed for any shortcoming in delivering the message and that the fault is theirs; Abu Hayyan also notes that the message implies the coming of a destroying punishment. As for 'they cannot harm Him at all', Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi explain that their destruction does not diminish His dominion, whereas al-Sam'ani and al-Qurtubi take it to mean they cannot harm Him or take revenge on Him. A reading attributed to Ibn Mas'ud, 'do not diminish Him', is cited by al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari. Finally, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi take 'Hafiz' to mean a watchful guardian who records and repays deeds, Ibn Kathir a witness who keeps account of the words and actions of His servants, and Ibn 'Atiyya one who knows everything.

This verse states that when God's command came, He saved Hud and those who believed with him by a mercy from Himself, and saved them from a severe punishment. The most common reading identifies this punishment with the barren wind that destroyed the 'Ad. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take the mercy to mean divine favour, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy see the repeated mention of salvation as emphasis on how severe the punishment was, with some reading the first salvation as deliverance in this world and the second as deliverance from the punishment of the Hereafter. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi understand the mercy as the faith God granted them, a view also attributed to Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan by al-Alusi, whereas Ibn al-Jawzi reports both explanations. The number of believers is given as four thousand by al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, with three thousand also mentioned. The commentators agree that the 'Ad denied their Lord's signs and disobeyed His messengers, since rejecting one messenger amounts to rejecting all of them, as al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain. They followed the command of every arrogant tyrant, and according to Abu 'Ubayda the word 'anid means one who opposes by contradiction. Al-Sa'di and al-Jaza'iri stress arrogance and stubborn refusal of the truth, and Ibn Kathir reports from al-Suddi that no prophet was sent after the 'Ad without their curse being invoked through his tongue.

This verse describes the people of 'Ad who denied the signs of their Lord, disobeyed their messenger Hud, and followed the command of every arrogant obstinate tyrant. The commentators agree that disobeying one messenger amounts to disobeying all of them, since they share the same monotheistic message, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain, while Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the plural may refer to the category of prophets or to Hud alone. Al-Tabari and al-Wahidi take the word jabbar to mean the proud one who refuses the truth, al-Kalbi and al-Zajjaj take it to mean one who compels people to his will, and Ibn al-Anbari adds the sense of one who magnifies himself. Al-Tabari links 'anid to the polytheist who opposes the truth, while Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir understand the phrase to refer to the leaders and notables who drove the people to reject the prophets. On the word tilka, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi take it to point to the graves and remains of the people, which one should look at and learn from, whereas al-Alusi stresses the call to reflection. All the commentators agree that the curse followed them in this world and the next, and that al-Bu'd means destruction or distance from mercy. Al-Zamakhshari also explains that the phrase 'the people of Hud' distinguishes this 'Ad from the 'Ad of Iram. Al-Farra' reads kafarū rabbahum as they denied the blessing of their Lord.

The commentators explain that this verse announces that the people of 'Ad, the people of Hud, will be followed by a curse in this world that will cling to them, and that they will be cursed again on the Day of Resurrection. They attribute this to their disbelief in their Lord, which some read as denying Him and others as being ungrateful for His blessings. The phrase "Alā bu'dan li-'Ād" is understood as a curse upon them, a call for their destruction and removal from God's mercy. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy hold that "disobeying His messengers" refers to Hud alone, since rejecting one messenger amounts to rejecting all of them, while others include the prophets who came before him. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur note that "the people of Hud" specifies which 'Ad is meant, distinguishing them from 'Ad of Iram. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud see the repetition of "alā" and the name 'Ad as a way to emphasise the gravity of their case and to prompt reflection on their fate. Ibn Kathir reports, following al-Suddi, that every prophet sent after 'Ad was cursed through his tongue. Al-Sha'rawi distinguishes three curses, in this life, in the barzakh, and on the Day of Judgement. Al-Baghawi and al-Tabari explain that the word bu'd can mean distance from good or destruction, both meanings of the root. Most commentators focus on the meaning and moral lesson of the verse rather than on legal rulings.

God tells us that He sent their brother Salih to the people of Thamud, who called them to worship God alone, since they have no deity other than Him. He is the One who brought them into being from the earth, since their father Adam was created from it, and who made them its inhabitants and builders. Salih commands them to seek His forgiveness and then turn to Him in repentance, and affirms that his Lord is near and answers prayer. The commentators agree that the verse establishes monotheism through the arguments of creation and blessing, and that asking forgiveness comes before repentance. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the phrase istaʿmarakum means that He prolonged their lives, settled them, or commanded them to develop the land, and most favour the sense of making them its builders. Al-Farra, al-Zajjaj and al-Nasafi add that cultivation includes building houses and planting trees. Ibn Kathir and others take the creation from the earth to refer to Adam, while al-Razi argues that man comes from semen and blood nourished by plants, which grow from the earth. Opinions differ on the people's words that Salih was a hope for them: al-Tha'labi and al-Baghawi take it to mean they hoped he would become their leader, while Muqatil and al-Razi take it to mean they hoped he would return to their religion. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Atiyya note the variant readings of the name Thamud, with and without tanwin, reflecting whether the tribe or the people is meant.

This verse reports the reply of the people of Thamud to their prophet Salih, peace be upon him. They say that they had hoped he would become a leader and counsellor among them, but his call to abandon what their fathers worshipped ended that hope. The commentators explain this hope in different ways. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Qurtubi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Su'ud take it to mean that they expected him to be a noble, wise guide and a source of counsel. Ka'b holds that they expected him to become their king, since he came from a noble and wealthy family. Muqatil, followed by Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Baydawi, holds that they hoped he would return to their religion, since he disliked their idols. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi give similar readings. The question «atanhana» is taken as rebuke and expressed surprise. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi note that al-Naqqash's reading of the word as meaning «despised» is not established in Arabic usage. Al-Razi and al-Baghawi explain their doubt as a state of wavering between affirmation and denial, with «murib» meaning something that casts suspicion. Sayyid Qutb and al-Sha'rawi stress their refusal of reasoning and their attachment to ancestral custom. Several commentators also note the two forms of the particle «inna» found in the speech of the Quraysh dialect.

This passage records Salih's reply to his people, peace be upon him. He asks them to consider: if I have a clear proof from my Lord and He has given me mercy, that is prophethood and wisdom, who will protect me from God's punishment if I disobey Him? What you say will only add to my loss, or bring you loss. The commentators agree on this general meaning: Salih is certain of his mission, no one can shield him from God if he disobeys, and their words bring him nothing. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Farra' explain the word takhsir as misguidance, ruin and removal from good, while al-Tabari, reporting Mujahid, takes it as their own loss, that is the mercy of God that they forfeit. Al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Atiyya show that the increase of loss can be understood either as the loss Salih would suffer if he followed them, or the loss they would suffer by rejecting him. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur note that the conditional form uses the language of doubt in order to address deniers, though Salih is certain of his position, and they describe the statement as an argument aimed at confuting the opponents. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Sa'di add that the supposition does not cast any doubt on his prophethood. The commentators do not choose between these readings and emphasize above all Salih's steadfastness in the face of threats.

This verse records that Salih, after his people asked for a sign, told them that the she-camel that had come out of the rock by God's will was a sign for them. He commanded them to leave her to graze on God's earth and not to harm her, or a near punishment would seize them. The commentators explain that 'eating' means grazing and drinking, and that the prohibition covers slaughter as well as any other harm. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi report that the she-camel emerged from a particular rock after the people's request, and that attributing her to God honours her, since she was created by His power. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi add that the near punishment means three days of grace after she was slaughtered. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi note that the phrase may also mean a camel dedicated to God. Ibn Ashur sees it simply as a reference to the divine power that created her. Sayyid Qutb reads the particle 'fa' in 'so He will seize you' as indicating haste. The commentators agree on the core warning, and differ mainly on the details of the narrative and on the meaning of certain words.

This verse tells that the people of Thamud hamstrung the she-camel, the sign God had given to Salih, and that Salih told them to enjoy life in their homes for three days, for this is a promise that will not be proved false. The commentators agree that the three days were a respite between the slaughter and the destruction. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report, on the authority of Qatada and Ibn Abbas, that Salih announced a sign: their faces would turn yellow on the first day, red on the second and black on the third, with the punishment coming on the fourth. They add that the camel's young, which fled to the mountain of al-Qara, cried out three times, and this fixed the term. On the meaning of dar, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Nasafi take it to mean the land or city, whereas al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baydawi take it to mean the life of this world or the time remaining to them. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan explain that makdhub may mean a promise that is not false, or a promise in which there is no lie, and Ibn Atiyya notes that the word may apply to the threat itself. Al-Qurtubi draws from the three days a point for jurists on the period that separates travel from residence, without deciding it. Ibn Kathir refers readers to his earlier treatment of the story in the chapter of al-A'raf.

The commentators explain that when God's command came upon the people of Thamud, He saved the prophet Salih and those who believed with him through His mercy, and spared them the disgrace of that day. The verse closes by affirming that your Lord is the Strong, the Mighty. They agree that the deliverance came from divine mercy rather than from the believers' deeds, and that khizy means the humiliation and shame that struck the disbelievers. They differ over the meaning of 'that day': most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Atiyya, al-Razi and al-Baydawi, take it as the day of the destruction by the cry, while al-Zamakhshari and others read it as the Day of Resurrection. Al-Qurtubi also records the view that the conjunction wa is superfluous. All agree on the account of the cry from heaven or the cry of Gabriel, and on the three-day warning during which the faces of the people turned yellow, then red, then black. Al-Tabari gives lengthy narrations of these details but notes the weakness of some chains of transmission. Readers also differ on how the word yawmi'idhin is vocalised, a point discussed by Ibn al-Jazari and Abu Hayyan, while others focus mainly on the meaning.

This verse describes the destruction of the people of Thamud, who had hamstrung the she-camel and denied their Lord: a great cry seized them, and by morning they lay dead in their homes, fallen on their faces or their knees, as if they had never lived there. The commentators agree that the punishment was sudden and total. They differ on the source of the cry. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada say Gabriel shouted a single cry; al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu al-Su'ud and others say it was a cry from heaven containing the sound of every thunderclap and of everything on earth, which broke their hearts within them. Al-Razi holds that God may have created the cry in an animal's throat, or that Gabriel produced it. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain the masculine verb by noting that sayha means an outcry. On the meaning of jathimin, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it as dead, Ibn 'Atiyya as crouching on their knees, and al-Mawardi as caught during the night. For kaanna lam yaghnaw fiha, Ibn 'Abbas reads it as they did not live there, and al-Mawardi as they did not enjoy it. The commentators close by invoking distance from God's mercy upon Thamud, noting the reading difference over the tanwin of their name, which depends on whether the people or the tribe is meant.

This verse describes the destruction of the people of Thamud after they hamstrung the she-camel. A mighty cry seized them, and by morning they lay dead in their homes, as though they had never lived there. The commentators explain that Thamud disbelieved their Lord, meaning they denied His signs and His warning, and the verse closes with a curse, "far away with Thamud", meaning they are cast out from God's mercy. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi agree on the general sense of their annihilation and the erasing of their traces. On the nature of the cry, opinions differ: Ibn 'Abbas says it was thunderbolt, while al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi say it was the cry of Gabriel or a sound created by God, and al-Mawardi reports three views. On the word "jathimin", some take it to mean fallen on their faces, others kneeling, others dead or lying still. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi note that the feminine noun "sayha" does not prevent the verb from being masculine, since the word means a cry. On the name Thamud, readers differ between reading it with and without tanwin, either as the name of the people or of their ancestor, and both readings are judged acceptable. Few commentators draw legal rulings from this passage.

Angels came to Abraham bearing good news. They greeted him, and he answered with a greeting better than theirs, then hurried to bring them a calf roasted on heated stones. The commentators agree that the good news was the birth of Isaac, followed by Jacob, and that the messengers were Gabriel, Michael and Israfil, though the reports differ on their number: three according to Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr, nine according to al-Dahhak, and other figures are also given. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Qatada explain the word hanidh as roasted or well cooked, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and others take it to mean a fat animal whose fat drips. On the greeting, the readers differ between salam and salm, and al-Tabari judges the two readings close in meaning. Most exegetes report that Abraham's wife laughed on hearing the news, but they differ on why: some say she was astonished, others that she rejoiced at the destruction of Lot's people, others that she had her menses, a view many consider weak. All note that Abraham hospitably offered food, that the guests did not eat, which troubled him until they reassured him. Scholars draw from this the etiquette of hospitality: hastening the meal, serving the best one has, and returning the greeting.

The commentators explain that when Abraham saw that his guests, who were angels in human form, did not reach out to the roasted calf he had brought them, he found them strange and felt fear within himself. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most others report that in that time it was customary that a guest who did not eat the host's food was suspected of harmful intent, and that this explains both the disapproval and the fear. The angels then told him not to fear, and informed him that they had been sent to the people of Lot.

Al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi follow this explanation. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Razi, by contrast, hold that Abraham had already perceived that they were angels, and that his fear arose from the nature of their mission, since angels only descend with a punishment. They support this view by the phrase "we have been sent to the people of Lot", which is said to someone who recognises the visitors but does not yet know their purpose. Ibn al-Jawzi quotes al-Farra' that the guests also feared being taken for thieves. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi draw from the verse rules of hospitality, such as watching discreetly whether the guest eats and serving quickly.

The commentators also discuss the two verbs "nakara" and "ankara". Abu 'Ubayda, al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi take them as synonyms and cite the verse of al-A'sha. Some, like al-Biqa'i, hold that "nakara" expresses a stronger aversion. Al-Razi also records the view that "awjasa" means either to perceive or to conceal within oneself.

This verse tells that the angels, bringing the good news to Abraham, greeted him and he returned their greeting; he then offered them a roasted calf, but they did not reach out their hands to it, which frightened him, and they reassured him that they had been sent against the people of Lot. His wife Sarah, standing to serve them, laughed, and the commentators differ on why. Al-Tabari, al-Samani, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi mostly hold that she laughed at the heedlessness of Lot's people while the punishment was near, or out of joy that Abraham's fear had gone. Ibn Abbas and Wahb ibn Munabbih relate it instead to her astonishment at bearing a child at such an age, a view some read as an inverted sequence. Mujahid and Ikrima take the word to mean menstruation, which al-Farra and Abu Ubayd reject while most lexicographers accept it. She was given the news of Isaac and, after him, Jacob; the term "wara'" means for Ibn Abbas and al-Sha'bi a grandson, while others take it to mean "after". The reading of Ya'qub differs between the nominative and accusative among the readers. The commentators agree that the good news was given to both Sarah and Abraham together, and that it honoured her.

Sarah, when given the good news of Isaac, exclaims in astonishment: Oh, woe is me! Shall I give birth when I am an old woman and this my husband is an old man? This is truly an astonishing thing. The commentators explain that her cry is an expression of wonder rather than a curse upon herself, and that the final alif either replaces the first-person ya or marks a lamentation form. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi largely agree on the angels' reply: do not wonder at the command of God, for the mercy and blessings of God are upon you, people of the house, and He is praiseworthy and glorious. Opinions differ on their ages. Ibn Ishaq reports that Sarah was ninety and Abraham a hundred and twenty, whereas Mujahid gives ninety-nine for her and a hundred for him. Several scholars, including al-Razi, hold that her wonder concerned the ordinary course of nature and not God's power. The word ba'l means husband, since he takes charge of his wife, according to al-Tabari and al-Wahidi. Ibn 'Ashur sees her words as wonder at two old ages joined together. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari note that the phrase people of the house includes Abraham's wife. The consensus therefore lies in an elderly woman's astonishment at an unusual announcement and in the lesson the angels give her.

The commentators explain that when the angels gave Ibrahim the good news of Ishaq and, after him, Yaqub, his wife Sarah was astonished that she would bear a child while she was old and her husband was an elderly man. The angels rebuked her: do you wonder at the command of God? They added that the mercy and blessings of God rest upon the people of this household, and that God is praiseworthy (Hamid) and glorious (Majid). Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi agree that the verse removes her wonder by recalling the favours and marvels God granted to the family of prophethood, for whom events beyond the usual order are not strange. They differ on the meaning of mercy and blessings: al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya take mercy to be prophethood and the blessings to be the Israelite tribes descended from the prophets, while others understand them as greeting, good, divine friendship and leadership. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi favour reading the phrase as a statement of fact, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi also accept it as a supplication. On the phrase 'people of the house', they treat it as an address or a term of praise, and most, following Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, include the wife, while the Shia dispute this. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari also report differing accounts of the ages of Ibrahim and Sarah without deciding between them.

The verse says that when Abraham's fear left him and the good news of Isaac and Jacob came, he began to argue with Our messengers about the people of Lot. The commentators agree that the argument was with the angels and not with God, so the sense is that he was disputing with Our messengers. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that after the angels announced the destruction of the town, Abraham asked whether they would destroy it if it held fifty believers, and then lowered the number until five or even one. The angels answered that they knew who was in it and would save Lot and his family, except his wife. Ibn Kathir explains his conduct as coming from his gentleness and compassion. Al-Mawardi holds that the debate concerned the nature of the punishment, whether it was total annihilation or a warning. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan consider that the answer to "when" is omitted, the sentence "he argued" standing in for it. Al-Razi thinks the dispute came from differing views of the divine command: does it require immediate execution, or can it be delayed? Several scholars, including Ibn Ashur and Ibn Sa'di, stress that his forbearance, his anguish and his turning to God explain his plea. In the end the angels told him to desist, since the command of your Lord has come and the punishment cannot be turned back.

This verse describes Abraham as forbearing (halim), one who does not hasten to punish, as one who sighs often (awwah) out of fear of God and compassion for people, and as one who turns back to God (munib) in all matters. The commentators agree that the verse explains why Abraham argued with the angels about the people of Lot, after the fear he had felt when his guests did not touch his food had left him and he received good news. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that the argument was with the messengers sent to punish: Abraham asked whether they would destroy the town if fifty believers were in it, then lowered the number to ten, five, and finally one, and the angels refused each time. He then said, 'Lot is there,' and they replied that they knew best who was in it. The population figure varies across reports, including one of four million, without consensus.

The scholars differ on the nature of the argument. Al-Hasan links it to Abraham's words 'Lot is there'; Qatada and most others see it as a question about the number of believers; al-Mawardi also mentions the question of whether the punishment was total destruction or a warning. Abu Hayyan and al-Zamakhshari note that the clause introduced by 'lamma' has an omitted or implied answer, and that the present tense conveys the vividness of the scene. Ibn 'Atiyya observes that the argument is broader than a quarrel, and that al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi take the three qualities as the reason Abraham interceded. Al-Razi argues that the qualities show his tenderness and his hope that the people might repent and be spared. The meaning of awwah varies: al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir give several explanations, al-Mawardi and al-Nasafi stress fear of God, and Ibn 'Ashur sees it as an image of Abraham's deep concern for people. The sense of munib is given as one who returns to God, as in al-Tabari, or one who is sincere, as in Qatada's report.

In this verse the angels tell Abraham to stop pleading on behalf of the people of Lot, because God's command has come and the punishment that will reach them cannot be turned back. The commentators explain that this answers the debate Abraham had with the messengers about the inhabitants of the town. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that Abraham asked whether fifty believers lived there, then lowered the number until he reached one, and the angels answered that they knew who was there, that they would save Lot and his family except his wife, who was among those who would remain behind. They also agree on the meaning of the second part: when the messengers came to Lot, he was distressed by their arrival and felt constrained on their account, fearing his people's assault, and he said, this is a grievous day. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi explain that the word 'asib' means a day of severe trial and harm. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the exchange could be read as a request addressed to God or as a reply to the angels, and he says that Abraham, described as forbearing, tender-hearted and turning back to God, was moved by compassion. He also draws the lesson that one should not ask for what cannot be granted. The commentators differ on the phrase 'the command of your Lord': some take it as God's decree, others as the punishment itself. Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir relay reports about the population and the details of the debate, which others regard as secondary. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari stress that the punishment was decreed and that neither prayer nor argument could avert it.

This verse describes Lot's distress when the angels came to him in the form of handsome young men. Their arrival grieved him and he was sore troubled, because he took them for humans and feared for them from his people, who committed the abomination, so he said: this is a distressing day. The commentators agree that « sayyi'a bihim » means he was grieved by their coming, and that « dhar'an » means his capacity and resources were overwhelmed. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report from Ibn Abbas and Qatada that Lot feared for his guests because of his people's conduct. Al-Mawardi offers another reading, that Lot had a bad opinion of the envoys and feared for himself, which he cites without deciding between them. On the word « 'asib », the commentators quote Arabic verses and take it to mean a hard, harsh day that grips people with evil, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi link it to the root meaning to bind. Several accounts, given by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, add that God told the angels not to destroy the people until Lot testified against them four times. These accounts belong to the narrative background and are not in the Quranic text. On the main sense of the verse, the commentaries agree: the guests' arrival plunges Lot into distress out of fear for them from his people.

This verse describes the people of Lot coming to him in haste, though they had long been practising the abomination of having intercourse with men. Lot tells them that here are his daughters, who are purer for them; they should fear God and not shame him regarding his guests; is there not among them one upright man? The commentators agree that ihra' means rushing eagerly, and that the sin meant is intercourse with males. Lot's offer, they say, was an attempt to shield his guests and turn the crowd away. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that 'daughters' refers to the women of his nation, since every prophet is a father to his people, as Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr say; Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada take it to mean his own daughters. Al-Mawardi notes these readings and a third, that the offer was only a display of humility. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan discuss the meaning of 'purer' and the grammar of the sentence. Several commentators, including Ibn Kathir, raise the question of a Muslim woman marrying a non-believer: al-Hasan holds it was lawful in an earlier law and later abrogated. Being disgraced is explained as being humiliated or put to shame. The closing question is taken by the exegetes as a sharp rebuke to a people with no reasonable man among them.

This passage gives the reply of Lot's people when he offered them his daughters. They tell him that he knows they have no need of the women and no claim to them, and that he knows what they want, namely men. The commentators broadly agree that the apparent meaning is that they have no desire for women and seek the vice with men. Al-Tabari and Ibn Ishaq explain that the daughters are not wives for them, while Ibn Kathir and al-Suddi state that they want only men.

Opinions differ on the word "right". Al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn al-Jawzi take it to mean need or desire, whereas al-Kalbi and Ibn Qutayba take it to mean lawful marriage. On the daughters, Qatada and Ibn Abbas understand them as his own daughters, while Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr understand the women of his people, since a prophet is a father to his community. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that Lot offered his daughters to protect his guests, and that marrying unbelievers was permitted in his law, a point Ibn Kathir and al-Razi tie to a later abrogation.

The commentators agree on what follows: Lot then says that if he had strength or a firm support he would repel them. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi note that his words had no effect on them. The hadith transmitted from Abu Hurayra, that God has mercy on Lot who sheltered in a firm support, is cited by several, including Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi.

Lot, having been confronted by his people who insisted on pursuing his guests and ignored his advice, wishes that he had the strength to repel them or a powerful kin-group to shelter him. Most commentators understand the 'strength' as men, helpers or personal power, and the 'strong pillar' as a protecting clan or tribe. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi transmit this reading, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi liken that support to the firm base of a mountain. Al-Razi, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Sa'di also discuss the sense of strength, including physical capacity and the possibility of acting alone. All agree that the answer to 'if' is left unstated, which the commentators explain as a deliberate way of letting the hearer imagine the consequences, according to al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi.

The hadith transmitted through Abu Hurayra, in which the Prophet ﷺ prays for God's mercy on Lot who used to rely on a strong pillar, is cited by nearly every exegete. Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi take the pillar to mean God Himself, while others understand it as the support Lot had from God through the angels. Al-Razi and al-Alusi note that Lot's words may reflect human impatience rather than a lapse in faith, a view Ibn Hazm defends strongly. Ibn Ashur adds that the expression conveys the despair of a man who has lost hope in his people's reason.

Most commentators therefore see this verse as a sign of extreme distress, after which the angels reveal their identity and reassure the Prophet.

The angels tell Lot that they are messengers of his Lord and that his people will not be able to reach him. They order him to leave by night with his household, that no one should look back, and they state that his wife will suffer what befalls the people, since she inclines toward them. The punishment is due at dawn, and when Lot grows impatient they reply, "Is not the morning near?" The commentators agree that the departure should take place in the last part of the night, and that the prohibition on looking back means not turning to gaze behind or lagging behind. Dawn is chosen as the time of punishment because it is a time of rest, so the punishment is harsher. They differ on the readings. Most read "fa-asri" with or without the hamza, which al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi consider two synonymous forms. On "imra'ataka", the accusative reading of the majority makes it an exception from the household, so the wife is not taken out; the nominative reading, followed by Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, makes it an exception from the verb "do not look back", and it is reported that she went out, turned round and was struck by a stone. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari judge the nominative more elegant, while Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi discuss its grammar at length. The interpreters describe the overturning of the cities and the rain of baked clay stones, without settling the exact nature of the sijjil.

This verse describes the moment the punishment fell on the people of Lot. When God's command arrived, commentators such as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that Gabriel lifted their cities and overturned them so that the top became the bottom, then rained down stones of baked clay arranged in layers. There is broad agreement that these stones bore marks distinguishing them from earthly stones, and that the verse warns every wrongdoer. The meaning of the word sijjil divides them. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrima and al-Hasan take it as a Persian word arabised, meaning stone and clay, or clay baked like brick, a view al-Tabari favours by citing the verse of the Adh-Dhariyat about stones of clay. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi report other opinions: that it derives from sijjil, the written record, or from irsal, to send, or that it names the lowest heaven, as Ibn Zayd held, which Ibn 'Atiyya considers weak because of the description 'piled up'. As for the marks, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan speak of white mixed with red, Qatada and 'Ikrima of red lines, and others of seals bearing each victim's name. On the final phrase, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan record that some read it as a threat to the Quraysh, others to the whole community of wrongdoers, and others to the nearby cities.

This verse describes the end of Lot's people: when God's command came, He turned their town upside down and rained upon it stones of hard clay, layered one upon another and marked in the sight of their Lord. The commentators agree on the sequence, with the overturning of the town preceding the rain of stones, and that these stones were unlike the stones of the earth. The meaning of "sijjil" is debated. Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid take it as a Persian word arabized (sang and gil), meaning stone and clay; Qatada and Ikrimah say it is simply clay, and al-Zajjaj cites the verse "stones of clay"; Ibn Zayd takes it as the name of the lowest heaven, a view Ibn 'Atiyya calls weak since the word is described as layered. Others derive it from the word for a register, a casting, or a gift. On the marks, opinions differ: whiteness and redness, a seal, red streaks, or the name of each victim written on its stone. The closing phrase, "and it is not far from the wrongdoers," is read by Mujahid as a warning to the Quraysh, by Qatada and Ikrimah as directed at the wrongdoers of this nation, by Ibn Kathir as a general warning, and some take it as referring to the nearness of the cities on the route to Syria.

This verse tells Shu'ayb's people to give full measure and weight with justice, not to cheat others of their due, and not to spread corruption on earth. The commentators agree that the aim is to pay people their rights completely, without shortfall. Al-Tabari explains that cheating (bakhs) means diminishing what is owed, whether by measure, weight, or otherwise, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi understand it mainly as underpaying for goods bought, and Ibn Juzayy and al-Baydawi take the wording as general. Qatada explains the phrase about corruption as traveling the earth in disobedience to God, while al-Dahhak links it to short measure and weight, and Ibn Kathir adds that they also committed highway robbery. Al-Zamakhshari argues that the command to give full measure follows the prohibition of shortfall, to encourage it more strongly, and that justice means neither excess nor deficit. On the phrase 'what God leaves you is better for you', views differ: Ibn 'Abbas takes it as the lawful gain remaining after honest dealing, Mujahid as obedience to God, Qatada as your portion from your Lord, al-Rabi' as God's command, and al-Farra' as God's watchfulness, while al-Mawardi lists six opinions. As for 'I am not a guardian over you', most read it as meaning that Shu'ayb does not watch over their deeds but only delivers the message and gives counsel. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that this benefit depends on faith.

This verse records Shu'ayb telling his people to give full measure and weight with justice, not to cheat others of their goods, and then saying that what remains to them of lawful gain after rendering people's rights is better for them than unlawful profit, if they are believers, and that he is not their guardian. The commentators differ on the meaning of "what Allah leaves you". Mujahid, al-Zajjaj and others take it as obedience to God; Ibn 'Abbas explains it as God's provision or the lawful wealth He leaves you; al-Rabi' as God's command; Qatada as your share from your Lord; Ibn Zayd as God's mercy; Muqatil as His reward in the Hereafter; al-Farra' as God's watchfulness. Al-Tabari prefers the sense of the lawful surplus left after honest weighing, since the context concerns cheating, while noting that the chain of the Ibn 'Abbas report is not accepted by transmission scholars. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that none of these fully fits the wording and that the meaning is God's preservation of His favour upon you if you obey. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi hold that the address reaches disbelievers on condition of faith, and that the benefit appears with belief. As for "I am not a guardian over you", al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi offer several readings: I cannot shield you from God's punishment, I cannot keep your blessings for you, or I cannot stop you from cheating; al-Wahidi adds that he was not commanded to fight them or force them to believe, and Ibn Kathir concludes that he is no watcher over them, so they should act for God alone.

The Qur'an reports the mocking words of Shu'ayb's people: does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped, or that we dispose of our wealth as we please? Their words "you are truly the forbearing, the rightly guided" are, for most commentators, sarcasm meaning the opposite: a foolish and misguided man, as Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Zajjaj, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir explain. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Sam'ani mention another reading, in which they sincerely credit him with these qualities by their own estimation and wonder why they do not prevent him from forbidding them to deal freely with their property. Nearly all agree that "your prayer" means the ritual prayer, since Shu'ayb prayed often and his people mocked him when he did; a few take it to mean his religion or his recitation. On "dispose of our wealth", opinions differ: for most it is cheating in measure and weight; according to Zayd ibn Aslam and Ibn Zayd, it is clipping or cutting dirhams and dinars; according to Muhammad ibn Ka'b, passing off debased coins as sound; according to al-Thawri, withholding zakat. The readings vary between nun and ta, which changes how the conjunction is understood. Shu'ayb replies that he holds a clear proof from his Lord, that he does not do what he forbids, that he wants only reform as far as he can achieve it, and that his success comes from God alone.

The commentators explain that Shu'ayb, addressing his people with courtesy, asks them to consider: if he stands on clear proof from his Lord and God has granted him lawful provision, how could he disobey his Lord's command? He makes clear that he does not forbid them something he himself does, that his only aim is reform as far as he is able, that success comes only from God, and that he relies on Him and turns back to Him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most exegetes take the bayyina as clear proof and knowledge of the truth, and understand the omitted answer of the condition from the context. They differ on the 'goodly provision': Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and al-Tabari take it as lawful, pure wealth, since Shu'ayb was rich, while al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and others take it as prophethood or knowledge. On 'I do not wish to oppose you in what I forbid you', Qatada and Ibn Kathir read it as not forbidding what one does oneself, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan read it as not getting ahead of them in their desires. Al-Tabari understands inaba as returning and obedience, and 'Ubayd Allah ibn Ya'la as supplication. Several modern commentators widen reform to the purification of souls and society, and stress that success depends on God's grace.

Shu'ayb addresses his people, warning them that his opposition to them should not drive them to persist in disbelief and corruption, lest they suffer a fate like that of the people of Nuh, drowned, the people of Hud, struck by a fierce wind, or the people of Salih, seized by the cry and the quake. He reminds them that the people of Lut are not far from them, either in place or in time. The commentators agree on the general sense of a warning against obstinacy, and that seeking forgiveness and repentance are the way to salvation, for God is merciful and loving toward those who turn back. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report Qatada's reading of shiqaq as separation, while al-Suddi and Ibn Kathir understand it as enmity, and al-Hasan as harm. Al-Mawardi and al-Zajjaj explain the verb yajrimannakum as 'let not bring upon you' or 'let not lead you to'. Regarding the nearness of the people of Lut, Qatada takes it as nearness in time, while Ibn Kathir and others allow both meanings, in place or in time. Al-Khattabi and Ibn al-Anbari explain al-Wadud as one who loves his believing servants and is loved by them, while others see it as beloved to the believers. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that Ibn Kathir's reading with a damma has the same meaning, the common reading being more eloquent. The overall lesson is that the call to truth must not be abandoned because of hostility, and that repentance remains open to whoever wishes to return.

In this verse Shu'ayb tells his people to ask their Lord for forgiveness for their sins, then to turn back to Him in repentance and obedience, and assures them that his Lord is merciful to those who repent and loves them. The commentators agree that istighfar means seeking cover and forgiveness, and tawba means returning to obedience and giving up sin, the sins meant being idol worship and cheating in measure and weight. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain mercy as not punishing after repentance, and wudd as God's love for those who turn to Him. Al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi report that wadud may mean the one who loves His servants, or the one beloved by believers for His favours, and al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya mainly adopt the first meaning while recognising the second. Ibn 'Atiyya adds that God's kindness towards people is so complete that it resembles the conduct of one who shows affection. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir conclude that repentance is accepted even from disbelievers and sinners, since God's mercy and love require it. Abu Hayyan and Ibn Juzayy place the verse within the warning that precedes it, seeing it as a promise of acceptance after the threat against persistence in wrongdoing. Al-Alusi notes that seeking forgiveness and repenting come first, and mercy and love follow from them.

The commentators explain that Shu'ayb's people, unable to answer his arguments, pretended not to understand what he said, then threatened to stone him were it not for the regard they had for his clan, and denied that he had any standing among them. On their words "we do not understand much of what you say", al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi offer several readings: they did not give him their attention out of aversion, they scorned his words, or they understood but refused to accept them. Abu Hayyan notes that his speech was of the highest eloquence. On the meaning of "weak", opinions differ. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada, al-Thawri and Ibn 'Abbas report that he was blind, and the lexicographers note that the Himyar call a blind man "weak". Al-Hasan and Abu Rawq take it to mean humiliated, al-Sudi to mean isolated, and Ali ibn 'Isa to mean physically frail. Al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan mostly favour weakness in defence and power, a reading many find the strongest. The word "rahṭ" refers, for most, to three to ten people, that is, his kin. The verb "rajm" means to kill by stoning or, according to some, to insult. Shu'ayb replies that his kin are dearer to them than God, a rebuke that, according to al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, shows they valued his clan's honour over God's. The scholars agree that this reveals their neglect of the truth when it came from its messenger, and that Shu'ayb called them to repentance and to seek forgiveness while reminding them of the fate of earlier nations.

Shu'ayb says to his people that they respect his clan and hold back from killing him out of regard for his kin, yet they do not give the same regard to God, who is greater than any clan. The commentators agree that the phrase "you have cast Him behind your backs" means that they neglected God's command, paid it no heed and did not fear Him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the pronoun in "you have taken Him" to refer to God, while Mujahid, followed by Ibn Atiyya and others, takes it to refer to the message Shu'ayb brought. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi explain that the word "zihriyy" is a irregular relative form derived from "back", meaning something set aside and forgotten. Ibn Juzayy, al-Nasafi and al-Qasimi follow this reading. Ibn Zayd gives a different sense, comparing God in their eyes to a spare camel kept only in case of need. On the phrase "my Lord encompasses what you do", the commentators agree that God's knowledge and power surround all their deeds and that He will repay them. Al-Mawardi lists the meanings guardian, all-knowing and rewarder. Overall the verse combines rebuke, reproach and warning, and Shu'ayb is known for his fine reasoning with his people.

In this verse Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, speaks to his people after they have rejected him. He tells them to continue acting according to their position and capacity, announces that he too will act on his own course, and says they will soon know who will receive a humiliating punishment and who is the liar. He then bids them wait, while he waits with them. The commentators agree that the tone is one of threat and warning. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand the humiliation as a punishment that falls on the disbelievers, Ibn Kathir linking it to the Hereafter, while al-Mawardi reports from Ikrima that the punishment is drowning. Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy take the humiliation to apply both in this world and the next. On the word makanatikum, al-Tabari and al-Baghawi read it as deliberate steadiness, Ibn Abbas as their side or direction, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi as a state of power and ability. On the phrase wa man huwa kadhib, al-Zamakhshari explains that it refers to the liar in their own claim, namely Shu'ayb as they called him. Abu Hayyan and Ibn Atiyya debate whether man is relative or interrogative and prefer the relative form. On raqib, al-Tabari and al-Sam'ani take it to mean one who waits, al-Mawardi lists witness, guarantor and waiter, and Ibn Ashur explains it as one who awaits. Al-Zamakhshari also notes that the absence of fa before sawfa gives the threat a sudden, dramatic force.

This verse says that when God's command came, He saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him by His mercy, while those who had done wrong were seized by a blast, so that by morning they lay dead, prostrate in their homes. Most commentators agree that the punishment was a cry. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir report that Gabriel shouted at them and they died where they stood, while al-Tabari says it was a cry from heaven that extinguished them, and al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi cite both views: a cry that drew out their souls, or a punishment that came from the sky. Al-Zamakhshari explains that jathimin means remaining fixed in one's place, and that the phrase as if they had never dwelt there means they had not lived and moved about there. Ibn 'Ashur explains the use of the conjunction waw here: unlike the accounts of Salih and Lot, no fixed time for the punishment had been stated. Ibn Kathir notes that the same destruction is described elsewhere as an earthquake in al-A'raf and as the punishment of the day of the canopy in al-Shu'ara', and that these descriptions complement one another. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi see the comparison with Thamud as referring to a similar kind of punishment. All agree that the believers were saved by God's mercy.

The verse describes the destruction of Shu'ayb's people. Struck by the Cry, they lie dead in their homes at dawn, as though they had never lived there, and the verse ends with a curse: far away is Madyan, just as Thamud were far away. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya report that the Cry was the cry of Gabriel, which took their souls, and that 'jathimin' means lying prostrate on their knees or motionless. The commentators explain that 'ghanaw' means dwelling in comfort, and that 'ba'd' here means perdition, as al-Tabari, al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi state. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the common reading is 'ba'idat' with the vowel of perdition, while 'ba'udat' is attributed to al-Sulami and Abu Hayyan. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi link the two peoples because both were punished by the Cry, and Abu Hayyan treats the mention of Thamud as a digression. Al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi add that the cry came from above for Madyan and from below for Thamud. The commentators agree on the general meaning and the kind of punishment, but differ on the details of the sound, the reading, and the exact sense of perdition.

God says that He sent Moses with His signs, which are clear proofs, and with a manifest authority. The commentators differ on the meaning of the signs: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others take them to be the nine miracles, while al-Wahidi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan also mention the Torah and its rulings, though Abu Hayyan finds this reading weak. As for the manifest authority, many read it as the overwhelming proof, and al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Nasafi take it to be the staff, the most striking of the miracles. Al-Razi and al-Zajjaj link the word to the root of the oil used for lamps. Moses was sent to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they followed Pharaoh's command. All the commentators agree that this command was not rightly guided and led only to ruin. The verb yaqdumu means that Pharaoh will go before his people on the Day of Judgment and lead them into the Fire, and the past tense is used to stress that this will certainly happen. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Qurtubi explain that rifd means help or gift, and that here it refers to a curse added to a curse, in this world and the next. Al-Kalbi and Mujahid speak of two successive curses, and Abu 'Ubayda gives the word the sense of aid given to the punishment.

This verse says that God sent Moses with His signs and a clear authority to Pharaoh and his chiefs, yet they followed Pharaoh's command, meaning his path of denial and rejection. The commentators state that Pharaoh's command contains no right guidance but only error that leads his followers to ruin. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari, understand the signs as the miracles and the clear authority as the evident proof, with Moses' staff singled out because it was the most striking. Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy allow that the signs may mean divine rulings, while Abu Hayyan finds this reading weak because the Torah was revealed only after Pharaoh's death. On the word rashid, al-Tabari gives it as good and sound, al-Baghawi and Ibn Juzayy as guiding to the right path, and al-Zamakhshari, al-Alusi and Abu al-Su'ud note it may also mean a praiseworthy outcome, in which case the next phrase explains it. Pharaoh going ahead of his people into the Fire is taken by most as the continuation of his leadership in this world, and the past tense used for he brought them down is explained as certainty of the event. On the double curse, opinions differ: Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada see it as the curse of this world and the next, Mujahid as two curses, and al-Kalbi as drowning and the Fire. The word rifd is glossed as help or gift, giving the phrase a bitter irony. The passage closes the account of Pharaoh and serves as a warning against blindly following those who spread corruption.

This verse says that Pharaoh will go before his people on the Day of Resurrection, just as he led them in this world, and will bring them to the Fire. Here "awrada" means to make enter, not merely to lead to water. The commentators compare Pharaoh to the herder who walks ahead of his animals to the watering place, and his followers to the animals that come to drink. Al-Tabari, Qatada and Ibn Kathir explain that Pharaoh was the leader of his people in misguidance, so he will lead them into the Fire. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Razi note that the past tense expresses the certainty of the event. They also explain that "wird" refers here to the place or the approach one comes to, and that the blame falls on this place, since water is meant to quench thirst and cool the heart, whereas the Fire is its opposite. As for the next phrase about being cursed in this world and on the Day of Resurrection, al-Tabari, Mujahid and Qatada speak of two curses, one in this life and one on the Last Day, while al-Kalbi understands the worldly curse to be the drowning. The word "rifd", meaning aid or gift, is taken by Abu Ubayda to mean support, by al-Asma'i to mean a cup, and by al-Kalbi to mean an addition. These different meanings are reported without the commentators deciding between them.

The verse speaks of Pharaoh and his people: they were followed in this world by a curse, beyond the punishment of drowning that was hastened upon them, and they will be cursed again on the Day of Resurrection. What they receive, a curse in this life and the next, is a wretched gift, the word rifd being used ironically for a recompense. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi agree that these are two successive curses, one in this world and one on the Day of Judgment, and that rifd means aid or gift. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak explain that rifd is the curse of this world and of the next. The scholars differ, however, on what the two curses are. Al-Kalbi and Muqatil, followed by al-Wahidi and Ibn al-Jawzi, identify the first with the drowning and the second with the Fire. Al-Mawardi gives the curse of believers in this world and the curse of the angels in the next, while Mujahid simply says that a second curse was added to the first. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Atiyya read rifd as both gift and help. Abu Hayyan notes that it can mean aid, as in a hadith, and al-Mawardi cites al-Asma'i that the vowelling changes the sense, so that the word could denote the cup or its drink, making the reproach fall on what they will be given to drink in the Fire. Al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan also suggest that the verse continues the condemnation of Pharaoh himself. The commentators thus describe a punishment that follows the followers in both abodes, without a ruling on the precise nature of the two curses.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ that what He has related to him of the news of the destroyed towns is only part of their story. Some of these towns still stand, with their walls and remains like a crop still standing, while others have been wiped out like a field after harvest. The commentators explain that this destruction was not an injustice on God's part: the people wronged themselves through disbelief and disobedience. The idols they had called upon besides God gave them no help when the command of your Lord came; they only increased their ruin. The exegetes agree that "standing" points to ruins that remain and "harvested" to those that have vanished, though they differ on the details. Ibn 'Abbas takes the standing ones as inhabited towns and the harvested ones as ruined, while Qatada and Ibn Juraij see the standing as those whose walls survive and the harvested as those leaving no trace. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that the verse is an eloquent comparison with crops. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand tatbib as loss and perdition, as Mujahid and Qatada did. Ibn Kathir and others stress the severity of God's punishment and the lesson for whoever fears the torment of the Hereafter. These passages raise no legal rulings; their aim is to comfort the Prophet and to warn his listeners, and the commentators present the different opinions without choosing one over the others.

This verse states that God did not wrong these communities when He destroyed them; they wronged themselves through polytheism, sins and rejecting the messengers, and so they deserved the punishment. The commentators explain that the gods they called upon besides God could not avert anything when God's command came, and instead they only added to their ruin. Most agree that tatbib means loss and destruction, as Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd report, with Ibn Zayd taking it to mean evil and Abu 'Ubayda taking it as destruction. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada explain that the cities still standing are those whose traces remain, while the ruined ones are those that have vanished, and that the whole is a lesson. Al-Tabari sees in the verse a warning to the listeners that if they follow the path of earlier nations they will face the same end. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir treat the next verse as a general statement of God's way of seizing wrongdoers, whose seizing is painful and severe. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the warning applies to any unjust town and not only to unbelieving ones, and Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of Abu Musa about God granting respite to the wrongdoer before seizing him. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan note that these narratives are meant to lead the listener to reflection. Al-Shawkani and al-Alusi point out that commentators differ on whether the pronoun refers to the cities or to their people.

This verse states that God seizes unjust towns with His punishment, just as He seized the earlier peoples who denied their messengers, and that His seizing is painful and severe. The commentators understand injustice to mean polytheism, disbelief and sin. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari that God gives the wrongdoer respite until He seizes him and does not let him escape; al-Tabari reads it as a warning to this community not to follow the path of the earlier nations. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi hold instead that the threat covers every wrongdoer, whether he wrongs himself or others, and not only unbelievers. The recitations differ: Asim al-Jahdari and Talha ibn Musarrif read « idh » in place of « idha », a reading al-Tabari calls irregular and does not permit. On the ruins that stand or have been reaped, most commentators see a lesson for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter. Most conclude that everyone who has sinned should repent and not be deceived by the respite granted. No commentator draws a specific legal ruling from this verse.

This verse states that God's punishment of unjust peoples is a sign and a lesson for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter, and that the day is the Day of Resurrection, when all people will be gathered and all creation will witness it. Commentators such as Mujahid, 'Ikrima, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir agree that the phrase 'that day' refers to the Day of Resurrection. 'Mashhud' means that it is attended by all creatures, humans, jinn and angels, and according to some even animals; al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya transmit Ibn 'Abbas's view that the 'witness' is the Prophet and the 'witnessed' is that day. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that the nominal form 'majmu'' expresses the constancy of the gathering and is stronger than a verb. Al-Razi argues that the lesson requires belief in a freely choosing Creator, since those who deny the afterlife attribute events to astral causes. For 'we delay it only for a counted term', al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi take it as a term decreed by God, while Ibn Kathir takes it as the end of humanity's appointed time. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report that no one will speak except by permission, and that people will be divided into the wretched and the blessed according to what was decreed or what they did.

The commentators explain that this verse states God delays the Day of Judgment only until a counted and fixed term, so it neither comes earlier nor later. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi take the term to mean the end of the appointed period of the world, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari read it as the period itself. They agree that the verse introduces the description of that Day, when people are gathered and witnessed by all creatures, when no soul speaks except by God's leave, and when some are wretched and others blessed. The main disagreement concerns the exception "save what your Lord wills" regarding eternity. Al-Tabari, Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Kathir apply it to believers guilty of major sins who enter the Fire and are later brought out, whereas Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud offer other readings, such as an exception covering the time before entry, or the consuming and renewal of the damned. Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' discuss several linguistic senses of the particle "illa". The commentators describe the zafir and the shahiq as the loud and faint cries of the tormented, likened to the beginning and end of a donkey's bray. Al-Tabari also cites the hadith of 'Umar about destinies already written and each person being made easy for what he was created for.

This verse describes the Day when people will be gathered, a day on which no soul will speak except by God's permission, and when humanity will divide into two groups: the wretched and the blessed. The commentators agree that this division follows what God has decreed in advance, so that the wretched are those for whom wretchedness was written and the blessed those for whom blessedness was written. Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and Ibn Kathir explain that the people of the Fire will remain in it as long as the heavens and the earth endure, and that the zafir and shahiq are two loud sounds, resembling the braying of a donkey. Al-Tabari and those who follow him read the exception, 'except what your Lord wills', as referring to believers guilty of major sins who will leave the Fire after a time, while al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' take 'except' to mean 'besides', or to refer to the time of standing for judgement and the interval in the grave. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that the forbidden speech is useful, effective speech rather than all speech, while Ibn 'Atiyya restricts the prohibition to argument and intercession. Some readers omit the final yā' in 'ya'ti', a form known in the dialect of Hudhayl. The hadith related by Umar adds that each person is made easy for what he was created for.

This verse describes the fate of the wretched on the Day of Judgment: they are in the Fire, where they have sighing and groaning, a breath pushed out with force and drawn back in with anguish. The commentators agree that the verse expresses extreme distress and torment, but they differ on the exact meaning of the two terms. Ibn Abbas said that zafir is a loud cry and shahiq a faint cry, al-Dahhak and Muqatil said they are the beginning and end of a donkey's bray, while Abu al-Aliya placed the zafir in the throat and the shahiq in the chest. As for abiding as long as the heavens and the earth endure, most read it as the Arabic way of expressing eternity, as al-Tabari explains, while others take it to refer to the heavens and earth of the Hereafter. The exception, except what your Lord wills, has been read in several ways. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak took it to refer to sinning believers whom God will bring out of the Fire after a time, a view al-Tabari adopted on the basis of the widely transmitted reports, whereas al-Farra' and others saw it as a formula of divine will that is not expected to happen, or as a mere duration. The verse closes by stating that your Lord does whatever He wills, emphasising God's full power.

This passage describes the fate of the wretched and the blessed on the Day of Resurrection. Those who were wretched enter the Fire, where they have zafir and shahiq, sounds of anguish that some compare to the braying of a donkey, its beginning and its end. Regarding the phrase "as long as the heavens and the earth endure," commentators offer two readings. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others take it as an Arabic idiom for perpetuity, like saying "as long as night and day alternate"; others, such as Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan, understand the heavens and earth of the Hereafter, which will not pass away. The exception "except what your Lord wills" has drawn a wide range of views. Qatada, al-Dahhak, Abu Sinan and Khalid ibn Ma'dan, whom al-Tabari follows and prefers, apply it to monotheist believers guilty of grave sins who enter the Fire and are later brought out into Paradise, as in a sound hadith from Anas. Al-Farra', Ibn Qutayba and Ibn al-Anbari read it as meaning "other than" or as an exception that never takes effect. Ibn Abbas extends it to whomever God chooses to bring out of the Fire. Ibn Mas'ud speaks of the Fire consuming its people and God then recreating them. For the blessed, the gift is "unbroken", without end. Al-Razi argues that this verse proves the eventual end of the punishment of unbelievers, a view disputed by others, including Ibn al-Qayyim, who rejects the Fire's passing away and holds that punishment lasts as long as its cause does. The verse ends with "your Lord does whatever He wills," affirming God's absolute sovereignty.

This part of the verse describes the fate of those who are blessed: they will abide in the Garden for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, and the exception "save what your Lord wills" does not, according to the commentators, mean that the bliss will end. The gift is described as "unbroken", meaning uninterrupted. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read "su'idu" with a damma on the sin, while the rest read "sa'idu" with a fatha; both readings are accepted. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan report that most exegetes take "ma" to mean "man", so the exception refers to believers who sinned and whom God brings out of the Fire into the Garden, described as wretched when they enter the Fire and blessed when they enter the Garden, a view attributed to Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak. Al-Tabari judges that the exception refers to the time spent in the Fire before entering the Garden, while others point to the waiting in the grave or the Day of Judgment, or to the Divine will in general. Ibn Kathir stresses that the continuation of bliss is not necessary in itself but depends on God's will. Ibn al-Qayyim and others understand that the exception does not imply the cessation of bliss. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Abu al-'Aliya explain "unbroken gift" as a gift that is not cut off.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ not to doubt the misguidance of his people who worship idols, since they merely imitate their forefathers without proof or divine command. As for the phrase "We will certainly pay them their share without diminution," Ibn Abbas, transmitted through Mujahid, explains it as what was decreed for them of good or evil. Abu al-Aliya understands it as their provision, while Ibn Zayd understands it as their punishment. Ibn Kathir notes that any good deeds they did are repaid to them in this world, and that their final portion is punishment. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan treat "without diminution" as an emphatic qualifier stressing the completeness of the recompense. Al-Razi offers several meanings: provision, punishment, or the removal of excuses through sending messengers and revealing scriptures. Ibn Ashur sees the word "share" here as used ironically. Later in the passage, the commentators recount the story of Musa and the Book, where disagreement is presented as a common attitude among peoples. The verse concludes that God will fully repay every person for their deeds, for He is fully aware of what they do.

This verse consoles the Prophet ﷺ by recalling what happened to the people of Moses. God gave Moses the Torah, yet his people disagreed about it: some believed in it and others rejected it, just as the Prophet's own people disputed the Qur'an. The commentators agree that the 'word that had preceded' is God's decision to delay punishment and not to hasten the chastisement of those who deny. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that God set a fixed term for their punishment, and Ibn Kathir adds that God punishes no one until a messenger has been sent and proof established. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi understand it as a postponement of judgement until the Day of Resurrection; otherwise the matter would be settled in this world, by destroying the deniers and saving the believers. As for 'between them', al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and the two Jalals refer it to the people of Moses, while Ibn 'Atiyya considers it better to include both peoples, and Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn 'Ashur take it to mean the contemporaries of the Prophet. The pronoun in 'about it' most often refers to the Book or to the Qur'an. Al-Tabari judges that the doubt concerned its reality and divine origin, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi say the disbelievers among the Prophet's people are in doubt about the Qur'an. Al-Razi offers several readings of the divine word, including that God's mercy precedes His wrath. Most commentators regard describing the doubt as 'troubling' as an emphasis on its meaning.

This verse states that God will fully repay every person, believers and disbelievers alike, for their deeds on the Day of Judgment, and that He is fully aware of everything they do. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the repayment means punishment or reward according to what each person did, and that the verse closes the account of the nations who denied their prophets. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd and Abu al-'Aliya add that the portion due may refer to what was promised of good or evil, to punishment, or to earthly provision; al-Razi notes that all these meanings may be intended. The commentators agree that the verse contains both a promise and a warning, and that God's perfect knowledge guarantees a just recompense.

The main disagreement concerns recitation and grammar. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr read "wa-in kullan" with the light form of the particle, while Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and 'Asim read "lamma" with a doubled m. Al-Farra' and al-Shirazi take "ma" to mean "man" and the lam as the lam of an oath; al-Tabari judges this reading the soundest, whereas Zajjaj and Nahhas report that "lamma" can mean "illa". Al-Mubarrad calls the doubled reading an error, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi see the tanwin on "kullan" as replacing the omitted genitive. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the original form was "liman ma", one of the m's having been dropped.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ and those who turned to faith with him to remain steadfast in the religion and in obedience to what they were commanded, and forbids them to transgress the limits. The commentators explain that steadfastness means persisting in obeying the commands and prohibitions without deviating to either side. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, agree that the address is to the Prophet and to those who repented from polytheism with him, and that the verse reminds that God sees everything His servants do. On transgression, Ibn Abbas links it to making lawful and unlawful what God did not command, Ibn Zayd to disobedience, and Muqatil to mixing monotheism with doubt, while al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir understand it as arrogance toward others. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya stress firmness on the path of truth and perseverance. Several report that this verse was the hardest on the Prophet, which is why he said that Hud and its sisters had turned his hair white. Ibn 'Uyayna defined steadfastness as holding to the Qur'an, and Ja'far al-Sadiq as firm resolve of the heart.

This verse forbids the believers from leaning toward those who have done wrong, meaning the polytheists and oppressors, since that would expose them to the Fire, for they have no protectors besides God and no one to rescue them. The commentators agree that ruku' means inclining toward something and relying on it or approving of it, but they differ on what form this takes. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Juraij understood it as inclining toward the polytheists, Abu al-'Aliya as approving of their deeds, and Qatada as joining the polytheists, while al-Sudi and Ibn Zayd took it to mean flattering them and failing to denounce their wrongs. Al-Zamakhshari held that it is a slight inclination, which includes imitating their dress and manners, sitting in their gatherings, and praising them, a view followed by al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud. Ibn Kathir reconciled the views by taking it to mean seeking the help of oppressors to the point of appearing to endorse their conduct.
