Al-Razi argued that the forbidden ruku' is approval of their injustice and taking part in their ways, whereas associating with them to avert harm or gain an immediate benefit is not included. Al-Qurtubi notes that keeping company with an oppressor under compulsion is exempted. On the scope of the verse, most take it as directed at polytheists, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy extend it to other oppressors and sinners. Al-Shawkani discusses at length the duty of obedience to rulers and the conditions attached to it.

The verse orders the Prophet ﷺ to perform the prayer properly at both ends of the day, that is at its beginning and its end, and at hours of the night close to its end, and it states that good deeds erase bad ones, a reminder for those who remember. The commentators agree that one end of the day is the dawn prayer, but they differ about the other. Mujahid and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi take it to be the midday and afternoon prayers together, al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Dahhak take it to be the afternoon prayer alone, while Ibn 'Abbas, and in one report al-Hasan, take it to be the sunset prayer. Al-Tabari prefers Ibn 'Abbas's view that the two ends are dawn and sunset, Ibn 'Atiyya considers Mujahid's view the best, and Ibn Kathir and others take the verse to cover the five daily prayers in general. As for the hours of the night, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid say they are the late night prayer, while al-Hasan and Qatada say they are sunset and night prayers. On the good deeds, most commentators, including Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, identify them as the five daily prayers, while Mujahid identifies them as the phrases of glorification of God, and Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the wording is general while the bad deeds are understood as minor sins provided major ones are avoided. The verse is linked to a well-known occasion, in which a man had touched a woman without intercourse and asked the Prophet, who recited the verse; when the man asked whether it applied to him alone, the Prophet said it was for all people, as reported by al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Tirmidhi, though other transmissions differ on the man's name. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that some consider the verse Medinan and others Meccan. Finally, the phrase that is a reminder is taken by some to refer to the preceding commands, by others to the Quran, and by others to the performance of prayer.

In this verse God commands His Prophet to be patient, and the commentators agree that this patience covers enduring the harm inflicted by the polytheists and remaining steadfast in obedience. Some, such as Ibn 'Abbas, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, understand it mainly as patience in prayer, so that the 'doers of good' are those who pray. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi link the verse to the preceding command to stand firm and to observe the prayer, and they report that good deeds wipe out minor sins as long as major sins are avoided. Al-Tabari explains that the 'affluent' are those who were given comfort and were absorbed in the pleasures of this world. Al-Mawardi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi see the doers of good as those who excel in their deeds and perform them sincerely. The commentators differ on the two parts of the day: al-Tabari and Ibn 'Abbas take dawn and sunset, al-Hasan and Qatada take dawn and the afternoon, and al-Razi, relying on legal reasoning, also favours dawn and the afternoon. All of them agree, however, that God does not waste the reward of those who do good.

This verse states that earlier generations should have included people of discernment and virtue who forbade their communities from spreading corruption on earth. Only a small number were saved, namely the followers of the prophets who forbade disbelief and sin. The majority pursued the luxuries they had been given and were criminals deserving punishment. The commentators explain that the word baqiyya means excellence, virtue and sound judgment, with some adding a sense of watchfulness and fear of God, and al-Zamakhshari taking it as a verbal noun meaning self-preservation. All read lawla here as meaning why not, expressing reproach. On the question of the exception, Sibawayh and most commentators take it as disconnected, while al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and others allow it to be connected by reading an implied negation. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the verse as an exhortation to this community to have people who enjoin good and forbid evil. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya reject any idea that God destroys unjustly; the destroyed towns wronged themselves through polytheism and sin. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that some scholars hold that a community which does not associate partners but reforms its own affairs is not destroyed for polytheism alone. Al-Tabari reports that what they were made to enjoy means what they were allowed to indulge in, while Mujahid understands it as arrogance in power and abandoning the truth. The commentators then link the differences among people to divine mercy: those whom God shows mercy do not disagree, and some say God created people for mercy and others for disagreement.

This verse states that God does not destroy towns unjustly while their people are upright, and that He destroys them only when they act wrongfully and the proof has reached them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and most commentators take injustice here to mean polytheism: God does not destroy a people merely for associating partners with Him as long as they deal justly among themselves and wrong no one, and destruction follows when they wrong each other. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud add that the rights of people are built on strictness while the rights of God rest on leniency, and that states can survive unbelief but not injustice; Ibn 'Atiyya reports this view and judges it weak. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur take the verse as affirming God's purity from injustice, since destroying righteous people would itself be wrong, and Ibn 'Ashur specifies that the destruction meant is the sudden annihilation of towns, not the general laws by which nations pass away.

Others, such as al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Qayyim, allow both readings: the injustice may be the people's own, as with the people of Lot and Shu'ayb who were punished for fraud and immorality, or a past wrong from which the people had repented. Ibn Sa'di summarises that God destroys only those who act unjustly after the proof has come to them, and may pardon those who return and make amends.

The commentators thus agree on the general principle: a community that keeps to righteousness is not annihilated, and the presence of those who forbid corruption protects a city, as al-Jaza'iri and Sayyid Qutb note.

God states that had He willed, He could have made mankind one single community, but He did not will it, so people continue to differ in their religions and opinions, except those whom their Lord has shown mercy and guided to the truth, who do not differ about it. The commentators agree that the divine will here is a will that did not impose unity upon the right guidance, and that the blamed divergence concerns the foundations of religion.

Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy explain that it is the religions, such as Jews, Christians and Magians, that diverge, and that those excepted are the believers or the adherents of the hanif faith. Ibn 'Abbas sees it as the difference between the people of truth and the people of falsehood, while 'Ikrima relates it to desires. Al-Hasan al-Basri speaks of divergence in livelihood, some being rich and others poor, the excepted being those content with little. Ibn 'Atiyya considers this reading far from the sense of the verse.

On the phrase "and for that He created them", opinions differ. Al-Hasan and 'Ata' take it as "for divergence", whereas Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak say "for mercy". Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan hold that the reference includes both at once: some created for mercy and others for divergence, a view reported by al-Razi and Ibn Kathir from Ibn 'Abbas and Malik. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi link this reading to free choice, while al-Shinqiti distinguishes the decreeing will from the commanding will.

The fulfilled word, "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men", is understood as a threat that is carried out, according to Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi.

This part of the verse states that had your Lord willed, He would have made mankind a single community upon one religion, yet people will continue to differ in their creeds, paths and desires, except those whom your Lord has shown mercy by guiding them to the truth, and who therefore do not differ about it. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and 'Ata' take this exception to mean the people of truth and the believers, while Ibn 'Abbas holds that the divergence covers truth and falsehood, and al-Hasan understands it as a divergence in provision and circumstances. As for the phrase "and for that He created them," the commentators differ: al-Hasan and 'Ata' take it to mean for the divergence itself, Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean for mercy, while al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi regard it as covering both. Ibn 'Abbas and Malik report that God created one group for His Garden and another for His Fire, a view al-Sam'ani attributes to Abu 'Ubayd and the people of the Sunna. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi explain that the divergence results from the choice God gave people, so the lam expresses consequence. The statement that the word of your Lord is fulfilled, that He will fill Hell with jinn and people, is read by all as a warning, though the scholars differ on who is meant, some pointing to the rebellious and others to the followers of Iblis. Ibn 'Abbas and others also link the exception to the people of truth who do not dispute in the fundamentals of faith.

God tells His Prophet that He relates to him the stories of the earlier messengers in order to strengthen his heart, to firm him in delivering the message and in bearing harm. The commentators explain that these accounts show him that the messengers before him faced from their peoples what he now faces. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report, with most exegetes, that "in this" refers to this surah, and that singling it out is an honour which does not mean that the truth did not come in other surahs. Al-Hasan and Qatada, however, say it refers to this world, meaning prophethood. Al-Razi and others explain that strengthening the heart means increasing its certainty and tranquillity, since the accumulation of proofs makes the heart firmer, while Ibn Abbas and Ibn Juraij speak of making him steadfast and of encouraging patience. Grammarians disagree on the role of the word "kullan": some make it the object of "naqussu", others an absolute infinitive or an adverb of manner. The verse closes by noting that the exhortation and reminder benefit the believers in particular, since they are the ones who take heed from the stories of the peoples who denied, while the verses that follow address the unbelievers with a warning.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to say to those who do not believe: act according to your position, and we act according to ours; wait, and we too are waiting. The commentators agree that the imperative here is a threat and warning rather than a permission. Al-Tabari explains that the waiting concerns what Satan promises them, while Ibn 'Abbas took it to mean their destruction. Ibn Kathir says the believers await God's mercy and the unbelievers await punishment, and he notes that God fulfilled His promise by granting victory to His messenger. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi understand the waiting as awaiting the calamities that will strike the opponents as they struck their predecessors. Ibn al-Jawzi reports that some scholars regarded the verse as abrogated by the verse of the sword, but that if it is read as a threat there is no abrogation; al-Razi likewise sees it as a threat without any abrogation. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy also read it as a threat. The next verse says that the unseen of the heavens and the earth belongs to God alone, that all affairs return to Him, so He alone is to be worshipped and relied upon, and that He is never unaware of what people do. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari note that these words are taken to close the surah of Hud, as reported from Ka'b al-Ahbar.

God instructs His Prophet to tell those who do not believe: act according to your position, we act according to ours, and wait, we too are waiting. The commentators agree that the verse is a threat and a warning to the disbelievers. Ibn 'Abbas, followed by al-Tha'labi and al-Qurtubi, explains that the waiting refers to the ruin and punishment of the unbelievers. Ibn Jurayj, cited by al-Tabari, reads it differently: the disbelievers await Satan's promises while the believers await the victory God has promised. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir specify that the believers await God's mercy and the disbelievers His wrath. Al-Baydawi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi understand that the believers await the calamities that will befall the disbelievers, as they befell similar peoples before them. Al-Zamakhshari follows this line. Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and al-Shawkani report that some scholars held the verse abrogated by the verse of the sword, while others, including al-Razi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Alusi, hold that there is no abrogation if the verse is read as a threat. Al-Sha'rawi sees the believers' waiting as a strengthening of their hearts, since those who speak this way are confident in what they announce.

This verse states that knowledge of the unseen in the heavens and earth belongs to God alone, and that all matters return to Him on the Day of Judgment. It commands the Prophet ﷺ to worship Him and rely upon Him, and assures that his Lord is not heedless of what people do. The commentators regard it as the closing verse of Surah Hud, following the stories of the prophets and the warnings to the disbelievers.

Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that the unseen refers to what is hidden from creatures, and that God will reward both the doer of good and the doer of evil. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak take it to mean the treasures of the heavens and earth or all that is hidden from the servants, while others understand it as the descent of punishment from the sky and its emergence from the earth; Abu 'Ali al-Farisi prefers the latter, treating the wording as a broad extension of speech.

The commentators agree that placing worship before trust shows that trust is of no benefit without worship, and that God suffices those who rely on Him. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi note that the particle 'fa' marks the consequence of the statement that all affairs return to God. On the readings, Nafi' and Hafs read 'yurja'u' in the passive, while the rest read 'yarji'u'; several read 'ta'malun' in the second person, others 'ya'malun' in the third.

Ka'b al-Ahbar reports that the end of the Torah matches the end of Hud, and some hadiths cited about the merits of the surah are not accepted by all scholars. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi see the verse as consoling the Prophet and warning the disbelievers, while Ibn 'Ashur regards it as a comprehensive conclusion summing up the surah.
